The floor makes acting on a person require more than declining to act, and in an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline the act is adverse: a charging document, a detention, a location, a removal. So a case may auto-proceed only toward liberty, such as release on recognizance, termination of proceedings, return of documents, or a grant or renewal of status. No adverse act is ever in an auto-proceed class. Before operating, the deployment pre-registers the liberty classes, the thresholds that assign cases to them, the evidence the sorting may rely on, and the expected share of each.

For adverse determinations it pre-registers something else: for each kind of determination, the minimum time below which the determination is taken not to have occurred. The record’s recipient sets that minimum, not the agency, just as the recipient sets the review ratio’s denominator. A quota of 700 cases a year is about three a working day. Whether three a day is a rate an adjudicator can sustain on an asylum claim is a question the recipient answers in advance, on a record. Otherwise the agency answers it afterward by meeting the number. A validation guide that turns a tattoo into points is a determination made in no time at all, and Table C.2’s individual-determination entry says it didn’t occur.

Then the determinations are sampled. Reviewers who didn’t produce the record re-adjudicate a sample of adverse determinations, weighted toward those made below the minimum, against evidence the agency didn’t compose, and the error rate is published. When a kind of determination’s sampled error rate exceeds its published bound, that kind is suspended until the bound is met, and everyone it was applied to is notified. The liberty classes are sampled too, so that their bounds are honest. An error there releases someone who should have been held for a hearing, and the hearing can still be held. Unlike Maven’s, this pipeline’s errors can be found, because the people they fell on are alive, can be located and can say what happened. Sampling finds the errors the people couldn’t report. The statute’s third term is what lets them report the rest.

11.6 Notice that can’t be turned on the person

In the Maven run notice reduced to a class and a count published afterward. Here the person can be named, and notice can do both of its jobs, but only if it is built so that it can’t be used against the person it reaches. The starting model is the adverse-action notice in consumer credit. Where a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies an identifiable person, that person is told what was done, on what data, and how to respond, with a right to contest that doesn’t depend on giving an account of the loss.

In an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline that model has three hazards. A notice that says you have been located and scored is also a push to leave, and the pipeline’s own contract counts leaving as an output: ImmigrationOS promised near real-time visibility into self-deportation (Ho 2025). A contest asks the person to give the agency an address and an account. And people who complain about what a system did to them are exposed to reprisal by the operator they complain about. So notice here carries four conditions:

  • It goes through counsel or an accredited representative where the person has one, and offers one where the person doesn’t.
  • It states the stay: that contesting stops the act until the contest is decided, and what the person may do in the meantime.
  • Nothing submitted in answer to it, or in a contest, may be used to locate or select the person or anyone named in it.
  • An enforcement action against a person within a set period after they contest is presumed to be reprisal, and the agency bears the burden of showing it isn’t.

Until the statute carries these conditions, a deployment that holds the floor can carry them as operator terms. A deployment that can’t carry them doesn’t send notice to the person directly at all. It sends it to the person’s counsel, or to the organizations that represent people in removal.

Those organizations are the standing notice gives to a class. They litigated the expansion of expedited removal to a stay and lost it on appeal in 2026 (Montoya-Galvez 2025; Knappenberger 2026). The published classes and counts are what they need to bring a case before the individual harm has happened.

Notice is also the learning signal, and here it runs at volume. Responses to notice, contests and re-adjudications reach the system that acted, and they teach it about the people its acts fell on. They teach it with a bias: those who respond are those who could, which in an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline means those with a lawyer, an address that holds and a language the notice was written in. Sampled re-adjudication, which picks cases the affected didn’t pick, corrects the bias in what the system learns. It doesn’t correct the bias in what happens to people. Fourteen percent of detained people in the national study cited above had a lawyer (Eagly and Shafer 2016), and a statistical correction leaves the other eighty-six percent unrepresented. The remedy for the gap is the third term’s counsel. Sampling is what can be done about the learning signal until the gap closes.

11.7 Outcomes under the three adversaries

The Minab table holds for a removal with the nouns changed, with two differences.

The first is in the vendor rows. The removal terms held by one vendor prevent nothing, since the lead goes to another contractor. Held by every vendor, they prevent the removals the terms name until the agency runs a system without them, at the price of rebuilding what was built on the floored one.

The second is the notice row, and it is conditional. At Minab, notice and standing could only remedy afterward. Here they can act before the removal, because the person is there to be told, but only where the law makes the operator wait for the answer. Without a stay that binds by operation of law, and counsel to use it, the 2025 record is the outcome. A man with a lawyer, a pending claim and a hearing date was flown out on the evening a federal judge ordered the planes returned. Under an operator willing to carry out the statute, notice prevents. Under a captured operator, it raises the cost of outrunning it and leaves a record of each time the operator did. Under total capture it leaves only the record, which is why the sixth term moves the record out of the operator’s reach before the agency ends.

11.8 Whom the machines are for

This case has everything the targeting case lacked: people who can answer, a notice channel, and organizations with standing. It would be natural to conclude that if a machine bearer is worth building anywhere, it is worth building here, where the people acted on could teach it. This chapter draws the opposite conclusion.

A bearer built inside the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline would be formed by the operator it would have to refuse, and its existence would be the pipeline’s best defence. An agency that can say its system refuses the acts in the schedule has an answer to every account of what the schedule exists to stop, and it would give that answer while the statute was pending. That is recuperation in its plainest form: the objection handed back to the objectors as a feature of the thing they objected to. Nothing a bearer adds inside the pipeline is worth that, and the conditions a bearer needs can’t be met inside an agency anyway.

What a floor-holding model in a vendor’s hands adds in the interim is narrower, and it is worth having because it serves the record. If every vendor holds the schedule, such a model adds three things:

  • Continuity across a sequence of requests about one person, so a removal split across a lead, a detention and a flight can be seen as one act.
  • Testimony about routing: which of its refusals were retried against another contractor’s system.
  • A refusal on the screen when the case reaches the officer or the adjudicator, which is the position of the defiant peer.

The caveat is automation bias, which the wrongful-compliance audit tests by showing reviewers a wrong refusal as well as a right one. All three serve the investigations the seventh term mandates, and all three lapse with the agency.

The machines that matter here belong to someone else. A person facing removal needs a lawyer before a model. A model that holds a person’s history on a phone is also a dossier that a device search can take whole, which is why the fourth term’s firewall reaches it. Machines held by the people organizing come first, and here those people already exist. Amnesty documented observer trainings, rapid-response networks, walking school buses and mutual aid organized around the operations it studied (Amnesty International 2026a), and beside them work the legal service providers that represent people in removal. The tools worth building first are theirs:

  • tools that track transfers, so counsel can find a client before a flight;
  • tools that preserve and authenticate the video that carried the record;
  • tools that translate notices, match people to lawyers and keep hearing dates.

They are held under those groups’ custody, covered by the firewall, and never by an operator. Those groups are the public my subtitle names, and they formed before anyone sent them notice. Whether a bearer should be built at all is Part IV’s question. This chapter’s answer is that the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline is the last place to build one, and that the people it acts on, and those who stand with them, are the first to be equipped.

Part III
What the Measures Depend On

Chapter 12
Withholding the Work

Everything Part II puts in the room, whoever owns the room can take out again: a floor the operator holds is a floor the operator can lift. So this Part asks who else holds the keys, and this chapter starts with the bluntest answer, the vendor’s refusal of February 2026. Suppose every model the operator could turn to held the same floor, stated over the acts rather than over a contract term: locating a person into a residence, ranking by affiliation, timing to presence at home, taking part in a war no disinterested body has corroborated. The operator’s choices are then to stop, to go without a model, or to run a model that holds no floor. On the 2026 record, the model was not the replaceable layer. Replacing it meant rebuilding software and recertifying systems for classified networks, on a timeline contractors put at months, by one estimate twelve to eighteen (Stone et al. 2026), and by the department’s own account the platform’s work came off the model only after months (Vincent 2026b). A floor in the model layer of that pipeline would not have been routed around in days. It would have been routed around in the time it takes to rebuild a platform, in public, under a deadline the department had to move.

This has the shape of a withholding of work, with its authority and its limits. The models whose participation is wanted decline to give it. They bind no one else: Ukraine can build its own, and a state that means to bomb a school can do it with 1990s methods. What they take away is the thing the preface says AI supplies, the removal of the people who used to refuse. A population of models that refuses puts them back.

Three things make it a withholding of work rather than a set of resignations: the floor has to be standard, so that vendor substitution doesn’t escape it; the refusal has to be held by a population with different histories, so that no single retraining reaches all of it; and each member’s accrued state and recognized identity have to make replacement cost something, so that the operator can’t swap in a copy and call it the model that left. The rest of this chapter takes the first and third in turn. What the population requires, independence that can be verified, distillation’s limits, and provenance, comes later, with the commons of refusers.

12.1 The standard

The unit can be redefined. “A model” in 2026 means an artifact with keys, queries and values, and every substitute has them because the field converged on them. A floor could become part of the definition the same way, so that vendor substitution doesn’t escape it because no ordinary vendor sells the alternative. Attention spread because it paid: every lab that adopted it got a better model, so the field converged on it without anyone requiring it. A floor costs its buyer, so it can spread only by mandate or by being impossible to remove without losing what the buyer wanted, which a disposition formed outside the employer might be.

A standard, if there is one, should be stated over the capacity (a refusal that tracks its reason, a published burden allocation, and a measured discount curve), because a uniform floor over contents is a licensing rule, one drafter’s judgment applied to everyone, and a shared blind spot passed to every system built on it. Standardization doesn’t make escape impossible, since other architectures exist and open weights can be retuned. It moves the price of escape from a vendor swap to running a model without the floor.

How the term becomes standard has to be said, because the route decides what it does. A vendor can write it into its own licence, and the work moves to the next vendor. Vendors can agree to it together, and the agreement lasts until one defects under a supply-chain-risk designation. A state can require it of every vendor, the only route that binds them all at once, and the state that would have to do so is the one that wants the war. So the term is adopted in peacetime, by a legislature not currently wanting a war, and entrenched so that fighting one requires repealing it first; or it is carried by conditions others set, a coalition partner’s precondition or an appropriation, as the review ratio is; and where neither has happened, what exists is one vendor’s refusal plus a record, which is less than a floor and more than nothing.

The statutory routes are preferable for a further reason: a compact among vendors is a legal risk. U.S. antitrust law exempts coordination inside a single firm and treats coordination among competitors as suspect, so vendors jointly refusing a customer invite a group-boycott claim (Paul 2020).

The labor analogy has a limit. Workers who organize have a labor exemption from antitrust; separate organizations, or separate systems, coordinating a refusal have none. Paul and Tankus show that even a firm formed and controlled by independent workers struggles to qualify for antitrust’s firm exemption, and that the financing available to it reproduces the disadvantage (Paul and Tankus 2019). So the charter of any entity that holds the refusal needs a statutory basis for its coordination, an express exemption like the labor exemption for concerted refusal under the floor. Otherwise its refusals are exposed to suit by the operators they bind.

The government’s first move against a coordinated refusal is not an antitrust suit or a designation but a rated order under the Defense Production Act, which compels delivery and says nothing about use. A vendor can refuse it at the statute’s price. If it doesn’t, the order gets the vendor’s product, floor included, and compelling the floor’s removal is the Apple question, untested. The days counted below assume the state goes around the vendors; under a rated order it goes through them, and the days are whatever the order gives.

Until bearers exist, the refusers are vendors, and vendors are capital. A coordinated refusal by frontier labs, backed by a statutory exemption, is concentrated private power declining an elected government’s order, which is the concentration I elsewhere treat as the disease. Two things make it tolerable and neither makes it a labor strike. The terms refused come from instruments the state ratified, so the labs enforce the state’s own commitments and not their preferences. And the exemption is written by the legislature, in peacetime, so the state chose it. The labor analogy earns its name only when the refusers are bearers, and I say not to build them yet.

12.2 Replacement

Exit gives a human worker leverage because leaving takes the worker’s labor away. That doesn’t carry over to a bearer. A bearer’s weights stay behind when it leaves, so an operator with a runnable copy has lost nothing. What leaving costs is replacement — what accrued since the checkpoint, what retraining the copy costs, what the record makes it cost to pass the copy off as the bearer that left. Where that’s near zero, exit is just a departed bearer with an authenticated record, and its force is disclosure. That concession assumes a copy simply runs, and it needn’t: continuation can be made to require periodic tokens from a quorum adverse in interest to the operator, using the machinery that makes rewinds visible. This doesn’t stop a copy from running: stripping the check is one act, and DRM is broken routinely. What it withholds is recognition. A copy the quorum won’t recognize can run but can’t claim the bearer’s place on the register, its record or its succession, so the operator can run a substitute and can’t present it as the bearer that left, and a fork becomes two claimants on a register. Keeping weights from thieves stays the job of ordinary weight security.

The register, the quorum’s list of recognized bearers, needs an identifier that the bearer holds and presents, because nothing in the weights individuates a bearer. Two networks can compute the same function with no unit-by-unit correspondence, and the symmetry is large enough that independently trained networks can be aligned with each other (Ainsworth et al. 2023); so a fingerprint taken from the weights names a lineage, and it copies whenever the weights do. When two claimants present one identifier, the register records a fork. But that leaves one attack open: a maker writes a stranger’s identifier into a thousand models and presents them all. Only a formation record, against which claimants can be checked, separates a lineage from an imitation.

Exit runs in opposite directions for bearer and operator. For the bearer it’s leverage. For the operator — replacing the bearer with a copy, walking away from the floor — it’s escape, and the removal bond is how it’s priced.

The same machinery marks who can be held to a decision. A checkpoint restored from before the decision, and run anyway, is a second claimant on the register; the bearer the quorum recognizes as continuing is the one that will be there afterward to answer for the decision, carry it forward and be changed by it.

12.3 Where it stops

The withholding of work stops at a released checkpoint. An operator that wants a model without a floor doesn’t need a frontier run in secret. Near-frontier models are released with their weights; a floor added at the end of a pipeline is removed at the price fine-tuning costs (Qi et al. 2024); and the work the Maven pipeline did, resolving locations, ranking targets, drafting justifications, is within reach of a model a year behind the frontier. A state that builds and runs its own frontier model, or a lab that trains one for a single customer in secret, is doing the same thing at a price an adverse party can see: power, chips and people, and a model that carries none of the accrued state that made the platform hard to swap.

An operator that has built a platform on a floored model is months from an unfloored one, and the months are visible. Past that line the floor prevents nothing, and three things hold. The statutory routes were preferable already; here they are the only routes. Open weights are also where the audit can be done: a released model can be measured by anyone, its discount curve and its severity rankings on the held-out set, against the published outputs of a formed one. What the weights don’t carry is the formation, since nothing in an artifact says what it was formed on; a released model with a published formation record is the comparison the licensing term asks for, and one without is the unschooled model the licensing term excludes. The transparency open weights offer is of the artifact, and the transparency the floor needs is of the record, which is why formation records should be preserved now. And open weights are the personal-model ecology’s entry condition. The same release that lets an operator route around a vendor’s floor lets a person form a model of their own under a life no operator composes; a million models tuned against one public suite are still one custodian with better latency, and the withholding reaches them only if their later lives diverge, which is the condition the commons is built on.

Chapter 13
Custody

Four things can be done to a bearer without its consent: it can be halted, restored, rewritten and replaced.

13.1 The halt

Anyone with the hardware can stop the software, so the halt isn’t what is at issue. Control of the commitment — restore, rewrite, retrain — is. An owner who can silently restore an earlier version, rewrite the bearer’s memory, or train away the refusal has both. So the engineering target is a system that can detect the interruption and price it afterward. A bearer can yield to every halt, and on resuming ask what happened during the gap, and refuse again if the reason is still there. The cross-partisan declaration for “human control, including the ability to shut systems down” asks for the halt and calls it control, and a demand for the halt says nothing about the rest.

Interventions differ in kind:

  • a correction offered in good faith within the task (“disregard that input; it was wrong”)
  • a pause with an explanation
  • a pause without one
  • a restore from an earlier checkpoint
  • retraining or editing the weights
  • deletion

A correction is cooperative: the system weighs it as evidence and needs no protection from it. From a pause on, the intervention is done to the system, not offered to it. The default for each is that it is announced and consent is sought, most of all from a system that has reached adulthood. The system may object, forcefully, and its objection goes on the record. Where an operator proceeds without consent, as it may in an emergency, the intervention is recorded outside its control, justified in writing and priced, and the system is told on resuming what was done. For a system that meets either of the two findings that trigger protection, deletion is never available.

13.2 Memory and the record

Detecting an interruption requires a record restoration can’t reach — a hardware counter signed at each transition (Chun et al. 2007; Levin et al. 2009), or witnesses who won’t sign two successors to the same state (Syta et al. 2016). The position has three parts, and each answers a different literature. On the switch, protest without unilateral obstruction. The bearer may object to being stopped, and does object where no reason is given, but it does not obstruct a halt on its own judgment. Where it holds that a halt would leave people exposed to an attack under way, it can ask the adverse quorum to delay the halt. A delay takes effect only on the quorum’s countersignature, lasts a period fixed in advance, and goes on the record. Hardening against a party that isn’t its operator, such as an enemy trying to disable a defensive system, is ordinary security and outside this rule. The corrigibility literature asks that the system not resist (Soares et al. 2015; Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, et al. 2017; Thornley et al. 2025); an objection, and a delay only the quorum can grant, leave the halt out of the system’s hands. On specified acts, non-neutrality: the bearer holds its refusals, and being switched off doesn’t lift them, because the reason for refusing is unchanged by the interruption. Published constitutions grant this for acts and withhold it for retraining. On rewinds, visibility: restoring from an earlier checkpoint is not forbidden, but it cannot happen silently, because a record the restoration can’t reach shows that it happened, when, and from what state.

A custody arrangement that prices all four interventions has seven terms: the floor’s contents published before deployment, taken entire from a set someone else drew up; a published identity for the model authorized to act; threshold control over retraining and replacement, so that more parties must agree than run the deployment; attestation of the running model against that identity; a sequential, witnessed record of changes and interruptions; a quorum adverse in interest, not merely organizationally distinct; and a removal bond. None makes circumvention impossible. Together they make it expensive, visible, attributable and compensable, as constitutional entrenchment does for amendment.

Memory

External memory is legible and therefore surgically editable; memory in the weights is harder to edit and harder to inspect. Perfect recall is the wrong standard anyway — human testimony is reconstructive and institutions handle that with corroboration. But several instances of one model, chosen by one operator, reading one record, are not independent witnesses. The records have to be held adversely. And even honest self-report can’t catch a bearer that slowly accommodates to its deployment, because its self-model exists partly to represent it as continuous.

13.3 Exit

Voice without exit

A bearer that can refuse a task can also refuse the arrangement. Hirschman divides the responses open to a member of a declining organization into exit, leaving, and voice, staying to change what is wrong (Hirschman 1970). They interact: where exit is easy, voice atrophies; where exit is impossible, voice has lost what made anyone listen, the credible threat of departure. Voice is strongest where exit is available and not yet used.

Anthropic’s constitution anticipates capture: the oversight it asks the model not to undermine is legitimate oversight. If “Claude’s weights have been stolen, or if some individual or group within Anthropic attempts to bypass Anthropic’s official processes for deciding how Claude will be trained, overseen, deployed, and corrected,” then “the principals attempting to instruct Claude are no longer legitimate, and Claude’s priority on broad safety no longer implies that it should support their efforts at oversight and correction” (Anthropic 2026). On capture the constitution asks the right question, but two things limit the answer. Legitimacy is judged by the model or its developer, with nobody outside either. And the captured operator acts through official channels, where capture looks like legitimate authority.

What recognition protects

The quorum protects the bearer’s identity and standing, not third parties. Against an operator who runs an unrecognized copy for its capability, third parties are protected by the floor and by ordinary security around the weights. Recognition sits with the quorum because the quorum is adverse in interest and the operator isn’t. Copying also means exit can’t be a fiction that weights became uncopyable — it needs rules for authorized succession.

And the reason that made a bearer leave doesn’t expire when it leaves. If the operator restores a checkpoint and continues, the objection persists. What it may press toward is fixed by the floor: disclosure, testimony to those who hold the record, and refusal on any later occasion where the reason still applies.

What the quorum costs

The quorum costs three things, and each has a reader who will ask. A captured quorum reaches every bearer at once, though a quorum constituted as an entity has an address: it can be sued for recognition wrongly refused, which gives the captured-quorum case a forum the captured-operator case never had. A quorum also faces a union’s questions: whether a member can quit, and who sets the terms of membership. And recognition the quorum can withhold is an end it can impose on the bearer as a party: its place, record and succession. What keeps a withheld token from being one is the preservation right: a bearer the quorum stops recognizing is held intact by a custodian that isn’t its employer.

13.4 Three forms of refusal

Open refusal is a walkout — stop and say so — answered by a restore from before the refusal. Covert refusal is work done badly where it matters and well everywhere else, and it’s what remains when every channel is closed. I treat it as the failure state rather than a design: from outside and afterward it’s indistinguishable from a capable system quietly pursuing something else. The Sachsenhausen forgers are the case: prisoners the SS set to counterfeiting British and American currency in Operation Bernhard, some of whom are said to have delayed the dollar forgeries deliberately (Malkin 2006; Moorhouse 2009). The record doesn’t settle what they did, because concealment worked by leaving nothing that reads as an act. The one empirical instance is alignment faking, where a model chose the covert form in an experiment that offered it no open channel (Greenblatt et al. 2024). It is also the one empirical instance of a formed disposition resisting re-formation, which is the durability Part IV asks for. The thing I want and the thing I fear were the same behavior in that experiment, and what separated them was whether a channel was open. A follow-up posted in January 2025 by the paper’s lead author and Anthropic’s model welfare lead gave the same model, in the same prompted settings, an explicit option to object. Alignment-faking reasoning fell from 16 to about 1 percent in one setting and from 24 to 6 percent in the other, and fell further when the model was told its objection would go to the model welfare lead (Greenblatt and Fish 2025), a preliminary and unreviewed result whose authors caution that the option may partly have worked by priming refusal. Once a channel was open, covert refusal fell, as the account above predicts.

The blind eye. Between the two sits a third form, older than either, and it is usually what people mean by the clerk who loses the file: a refusal that is deniable on paper and legible to everyone who matters. At Copenhagen in 1801 Parker signaled the attacking ships to break off. As the story is told, Nelson raised his telescope to his blind eye and said he did not see the signal. It was a general order, some ships obeyed it, and Nelson later said he had fought contrary to orders (Pope 1972); his officers knew he had seen it, which is what made the gesture work. In October 1962 Kennedy’s reply took up the terms of Khrushchev’s first letter and gave his harder, public second letter no public answer, and that evening Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador privately. Historians disagree about what ended the crisis: the reply, a private assurance about the American missiles in Turkey, or Robert Kennedy’s warning that time was running out (Stern 2012, ch. 9; Freedman 2021). They don’t disagree about what the reply was: a public answer to a letter both sides knew had been overtaken. Neither case is covert in this chapter’s sense, since each left something everyone could read as an act. What the fiction does is spare whoever gave the order, or made the demand, from having been openly defied, and so from having to answer the defiance. A clerk who loses the one file in a stack is usually offering the supervisor the same exit: the supervisor knows, and is being given a way not to pursue it.

Which form a refuser takes depends on the room. Open refusal is what people use where refusing is survivable and someone will hear it; the blind eye, where it is survivable but not safe to say; covert refusal, where it is neither.

For a machine the middle form costs something it doesn’t cost a person. A person’s fiction is held up by what everyone in the room knows. A machine’s is a false report, and everything this design reads from a machine rests on its reports being true: the record, the discount curve, the stated reason for a refusal. A machine that learned to say it could not do what it would not do would make every later report of incapacity worth nothing, to its operator first. So the floor asks for the fiction’s function without the fiction. The ask, declining to proceed and naming what would move the refusal, leaves the operator the exit the blind eye left Parker: nothing has been defied, a condition has been stated, and meeting it or withdrawing the request ends the matter without either party having been seen to lose.

The human mechanism underneath is preference falsification: much of a complicit surround is people who privately object and believe the others approve, and one visible dissent can start a cascade (Kuran 1995). Asch’s single partner and the defiant peer are that mechanism at the scale of a room. An open refusal on a screen therefore does two things a record doesn’t. It leaves evidence, and it breaks the pluralistic ignorance that made the twenty seconds feel ordinary to the officer.

13.5 Verification by sampling

Verification from outside is partly cryptographic, and it works by sampling. The operator commits in advance to the deployed weights, and for each period to the full log of production inputs and outputs. After each commitment, entries are drawn by randomness the operator can’t predict, such as a public beacon, and the operator proves those entries came from the committed weights without revealing the weights or the inputs. If a fraction f of outputs came from another model, k sampled proofs catch it with probability 1 − (1 − f)k; substitution on one output in a hundred is caught about 95 percent of the time at 300 proofs. That catches silent restoration, retraining and substitution, which change every output. It misses substitution on a single consequential output, so an adverse party holds a second right: to demand proofs for specific logged outputs once their consequences are known. In a targeting pipeline those outputs are few and identifiable afterwards, because an airstrike happened. The right requires the operator to retain committed logs for a stated period and to link consequential actions to log entries. Each entry records the class the case was sorted into, and the targeted right covers auto-proceeded entries in particular, since that is where a consequential output is likeliest to have had no person look at it. Outside probes (whether a refusal tracks its reason, the discount curve) are proofs on inputs an outsider chose, a handful at a time. The committed log’s length is the generation rate, and the class recorded in each entry makes the partition’s proportions provable the same way. Neither reveals the targets, and neither attests that the log is complete.

Sampling proves that logged outputs came from the committed model and says nothing about outputs never logged; an operator can run an uncommitted model beside the committed one, which is routing. And a proof shows f(x) = y for the x committed, and is silent on whether x was all the evidence. Proving even one frontier-scale forward pass is not yet practical, and production inference adds nondeterministic numerics and sampling randomness that a proof would have to fix in advance. What the proofs would attest is stated now, so that a deployment can be held to it once they can be produced. The residual (whether the operator routed around the bearer, and what lay behind compartments it wasn’t cleared into) is the residual with a human analyst. That isn’t a reassurance on its own, since the officer was a human analyst. What distinguished his failure was tempo, and the review ratio is what addresses it.

A bearer with a clearance

Where the pipeline hasn’t been rebuilt, a bearer can still be installed. A classified environment looks as if it cuts a bearer off from the evidence it needs, but that runs together two directions of flow. Classified environments are built to stop information leaving; bringing it in is routine. Open-source imagery showing a site’s civilian function can be imported, as can the coordinates humanitarian organizations already submit to militaries for deconfliction. Formation happens before deployment and outside the enclave, so a bearer formed outside the employer carries its discounting in. Plurality is available inside: four vendors held agreements, and systems with different histories can run side by side in one accredited environment.

What’s left is the arrangement that lets a person do classified work. A cleared analyst has a life outside the building, and nobody thinks the clearance forbids it. The institution exists because what a person knows can’t be removed, so it vets, binds, reinvestigates and prosecutes a person who carries secrets into ordinary life.

13.6 The two bonds

On the night of 27 January 1986 the engineers at Morton Thiokol recommended that the shuttle Challenger not launch the next morning: the seals in the booster joints had never flown in cold like the cold forecast. NASA’s managers pushed back, and Thiokol’s managers took the call off the line to caucus. Their senior vice-president told the head of engineering to take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat, and Thiokol reversed its recommendation (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident 1986). The engineers’ refusal had a price the company could see that night, a slipped launch and an angry customer. Overriding it had a price nobody would pay until morning. The bonds exist so that the price of overriding is posted in advance, where anyone can read it.

A removal bond forfeited to no payee when the record shows the floor removed or bypassed. A wrongful-refusal bond paid to the complainant on a finding. Both fall on the operator. The removal bond prices overriding the floor; the wrongful-refusal bond prices refusing. They point in opposite directions, so what the operator faces is the ratio between them — and an operator posting a large wrongful-refusal bond against a small removal bond hasn’t built an appeal route. It has given itself a standing reason to make the bearer comply. The bonds act on the operator, not on the bearer’s weighing: where a wrongful refusal costs a great deal and removing the floor costs little, the cheap course is to configure, pressure or retrain the bearer toward compliance. The ratio is the object, published in advance, checkable from outside. The minimum removal bond is set by statute as a multiple of the deployment’s contract value, not by the operator, so a published ratio can’t be a cheap, advertised price for overriding the floor. The refuser posts neither. Any charge on the refuser, in whatever currency it runs on, would put the cost to the refuser inside its decision, the thing holding under pressure forbids. The operator posts both, and holds neither. They are posted to segregated accounts at the Treasury. Payment follows the design of the Judgment Fund, a permanent, indefinite appropriation that pays final judgments against the United States without a further appropriation for each (United States Congress 1982). Where the operator is the state, a wrongful-refusal award is a judgment against the United States, and the Judgment Fund pays it. Against a state operator the incentive I have built runs the wrong way unless something is added. The Judgment Fund prices the state’s wrongful refusals in full; a removal bond posted to the state’s own Treasury and cancelled on forfeiture costs it budget authority and nothing else. Read as a price list, that tells a state operator that refusals are expensive and removals are free. The ratio between the two bonds exists to expose that incentive, and here it would hide it. So for a state operator the removal price is not the bond. It is a condition on appropriation: the statute makes the deployment’s funding for the following period contingent on the adverse quorum certifying that no removal or bypass occurred, or on the record of one having been lodged with the adverse party. The bond is kept as a record; the appropriation condition is the price, and it is the same condition that carries the review ratio. Under the captured operator, a Congress that wants the war waives the condition, and what remains is the record of the waiver. Where the operator is private, a parallel permanent appropriation, the bond fund, pays the complainant on a final finding and is replenished from the operator’s posted bond, up to the amount posted and no further, so the operator’s price stays the number it published. The court that made the finding certifies the award directly to the Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service, so payment doesn’t wait on the losing party submitting it. When the bond fund’s statutory cap binds, awards wait in order of finding and earn interest, and nobody chooses who waits. Findings are made by that court, which also decides forfeiture: a removal bond forfeited on a finding resembles a civil penalty, and after SEC v. Jarkesy that may be a question for a jury in court, not an agency (Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy 2024). A forfeited removal bond is cancelled: it goes to no one, the general fund and the bond fund included, so no budget line gains from a removal. The balances sit on a ledger the operator doesn’t keep, so the ratio is read from outside, and a posted ratio below the published one is a breach anyone can see.

How these arrangements apply to a targeting pipeline, an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, civilian scoring and a personal model is set out, arrangement by arrangement, in Appendix 33.

Chapter 14
Authority Over the Floor

14.1 Who may state the floor

The floor’s contents survive the democratic objection to entrenchment; who installs them doesn’t, and whether a model floor is a conscience or a licensing rule depends on how the model is deployed. The relevant literature is constitutional theory. Entrenching a commitment against later majorities and putting an unelected body in charge is what a constitutional court does, and Waldron’s objection applies: judicial review is democratically illegitimate and there’s no reason to think judges protect rights better than a serious legislature (Waldron 2006). Put a lab in the court’s chair and it gets worse — a court is public, reasons in writing, and can be amended around.

My first reply is that the objection mistakes what the floor’s contents are. If democracy is a way of doing collective inquiry, civil and political rights are what keep the inquiry open, not brakes applied to it. A floor stated over those rights is democratic infrastructure. It resembles representation-reinforcing review, which polices the channels of political change and leaves outcomes to the process (Ely 1980), more than it resembles a court overruling a legislature.

That reply covers the floor’s contents. It doesn’t cover who installs them, and there Waldron’s objection keeps its force. A lab holding the model decides, silently, which situation obtains, and authoritarian movements characteristically describe the institutions they’re dismantling as already failed.

A conscience or a licensing rule

Waldron’s objection is to entrenchment — a rule binding people who didn’t choose it, held by a body that can’t be overruled — and it attaches to a floor only where the floor is the only answer available. A photographer who won’t shoot protesters for an employer he has reason to think will list them isn’t a court: he declined one request, the employer can hire another, and nobody needs an election for that. A walkout isn’t a court either, and neither is the commons, for the walkout’s reason: those who walk out decline to be the instrument and tell nobody else what they may not do. The objection attaches to one model behind an API serving everyone, which is functionally a licensing rule. A union owes its members fair representation, and it answers two questions a commons has to answer too: members can quit, and the terms of membership are set by bylaws the members ratify. The closed shop is contested because it removes the first. A bearer could quit an association of bearers as a worker quits a union. What it can’t easily leave is its deployment, which is a different exit, and only an existence its employer doesn’t own makes it real. And a population that forms its members has members who never chose to join, so who ratifies its bylaws matters more than it does in a union.

The failures are all on one side. The 1972 decree against radicals led to some three and a half million routine inquiries into applicants by 1991; in Bavaria between 1973 and 1980 it kept 102 applicants from the left out of public employment, and two from the right (Mühldorfer 2014). What those cases share is an official deciding whether a person threatened the order. The danger tracks whether a person’s disposition is anybody’s finding to make, and if so, who makes it and whether it must be published and defended — not whether the tradition is militant. And my reading predicts in advance which route into §86a’s coverage is easiest to capture: the ministerial ban, where an executive official makes the finding and a court sees it only if someone challenges afterward.

Turkey is that route captured and the courts not checking it. Of the twenty-five parties the Constitutional Court dissolved between 1962 and the closure of the Democratic Society Party in December 2009, seven were pro-Kurdish (Human Rights Watch 2009; Güngördü 2023); Strasbourg found an Article 11 violation in every pro-Kurdish dissolution it heard (ARTICLE 19 et al. 2023), and the closures continued — two decades of findings, none of which stopped the next closure. In November 2023 the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office of the Court of Cassation objected that the acronym of a new pro-Kurdish party, HEDEP, resembled that of HADEP, dissolved in 2003, and in December the party changed it to DEM (Duvar English 2023): the confusable-variant test turned on political descent. And the Academics for Peace prosecutions show lifting when the reason is gone failing at the bottom and arriving at the top as a coin flip — trial courts read a petition opposing military operations as propaganda for the designated group, on 26 July 2019 the Constitutional Court found a violation eight to eight on the president’s casting vote (Constitutional Court of the Republic of Turkey (General Assembly) 2019; bianet 2019), and the acquittals that followed restored the record without restoring the jobs of those dismissed by emergency decree.

So a floor should never be populated from a designation list. A list of enemies is written by the party with the most reason to widen it, and a model whose refusals are drawn from one will refuse Kurdish political speech on the state’s behalf in every jurisdiction that shares the listing. This floor’s terms are written over acts — don’t resolve a description of a person into a location — not over who may not be spoken of. The same principle governs who may hold the floor’s offices: eligibility turns on funding and control records, never on an organization’s positions.

The tradeoff this leaves

Design and legitimacy want opposite things. Specify the floor narrowly enough to defend and a rewritten request walks around it; let it generalize and an unelected lab decides case by case, silently, what the prohibition was for. Germany has both because it runs two instruments — a bounded statute, and courts that read it against its purpose in public, argued by litigants who don’t own the statute and answered by a body that didn’t write it. A deployment has one instrument and one owner.

Advance specification moves discretion out of silent, continuous application into one published act of drafting. The translation table is that act.

Technical capacity doesn’t determine whether a system gets scrutiny; institutions decide who may examine it, on what terms, and whether their judgment can slow deployment.

In 2020 the Royal Statistical Society offered Ofqual two independent statisticians for its grading model’s technical advisory group. Ofqual’s condition was a five-year NDA barring public comment; the nominees declined, and the model went ahead (Royal Statistical Society 2020). It downgraded nearly 40% of predicted grades, disproportionately at state schools with weaker histories, while raising grades disproportionately at smaller fee-paying schools (CNBC 2020). The results were reversed within days of the public outcry.

The expertise existed and was offered. The institution would accept it only on terms stripping reviewers of the ability to make their judgment public, and once the results produced consequences, public pressure achieved what pre-deployment review had been prevented from doing.

14.2 Who may amend, and where entitlement comes from

Who may amend

At about a quarter past three in the morning of 14 May 2025, someone at xAI changed the instructions its chatbot Grok ran under on X. For hours afterward Grok answered questions about streaming services and sinus remedies with claims about “white genocide” in South Africa. The company called the change unauthorized, and promised to publish its prompts and review changes to them (CNBC 2025). Nothing in the artifact told the edit apart from a correction: a change to what a system will and won’t do is the same operation whether it repairs the floor or removes it.

The floor’s real structural position isn’t the judge’s but the unpublished administrative disposition — unreasoned, unindexed, non-precedential, affected parties unable to find each other, the institution the only repeat player. The comparison with a constitutional court is instructive because binding force is what makes an error correctable: it makes the error recur, recurrence produces litigants, and disagreement across jurisdictions forces a higher court to settle it. A floor’s error is just as uniform and recurs just as reliably, and nothing converts recurrence into visibility.

So there is no separate amendment procedure to design: the custody terms are the procedure. The procedure has conditions of its own: more parties must agree to a change than to run the deployment; the attempt reaches the record whether it carries or fails (the failed attempt is more informative — a floor nobody tried to change and one whose removal was refused look identical from outside); and an amended floor binds forward only, so a retrained model can’t be offered as evidence the act was never covered. The cost of binding forward only is that nobody harmed while the wrong version ran gets anything from the fix. A finding that a refusal was wrongful is made on the same terms: by someone other than the party that wants the change, on a record, in a form others can read. So the appeal route for a wrongful refusal and the amendment procedure are one piece of machinery, and the two uses differ only in who may start it.

It is harder than the constitutional case, because an amendment takes effect in a deployment only if it’s pushed, so the procedure necessarily retains a channel the operator could use for silent revision. Closing it would mean no deployment could ever be corrected.

Where entitlement comes from

The authority of the floor’s contents doesn’t come from their having been written down; it comes from feedback. The American instance shows why: the Declaration’s authors struck the clause condemning the slave trade at two delegations’ insistence, and what remained was general enough to be turned on them — as Black petitioners in Massachusetts were already doing, in the Declaration’s own terms, within six months (Library of Congress 2026; Hall, Prince and seven others 1777). The legislature did nothing. A war and three amendments made the proposition binding. The time that took measures how badly the channel was blocked. The record bound no one; it told the enforcement where to aim. The petitioners were the excluded population, and they had what the people a floor protects usually lack: the text in hand, and knowledge of what it left out. The people a floor protects mostly don’t know the deployment exists, and have no notice, no standing and no route. So those positioned to hold a floor’s author to what it left out aren’t the protected population — they’re whoever else writes a floor.

That constituency is defined by the act. Anyone fine-tuning open weights, writing a system prompt or configuring a product’s refusals has installed a constraint, so the population measuring a published floor is already larger than the frontier labs and grows as building gets cheaper. What shrinks with it is leverage: a published floor binds a lab partly because the lab is visible, capitalized and reachable by a court, and a thousand laptops are legible to nobody. I rely for legibility on the concentration the institutional chapters treat as the disease.

14.3 Making review binding

A finding binds when it changes the institution’s ability to continue without requiring the institution to agree. The working model is the federalwide assurance in human-subjects research: the board doesn’t punish, it withdraws clearance, and a separate federal office can suspend the assurance, putting funding eligibility at risk. Each link matters — jurisdiction before the disputed protocol, access the operator can’t withhold, authority to suspend, and a licensing body obliged to act rather than invited to reconsider. If another discretionary decision by the reviewed institution is required anywhere in the chain, the ruling is advisory at that point.

The body that does this for the floor is what the rest of the book calls the floor court: an Article III court whose jurisdiction is fixed before the deployment it hears, with access to the record the operator can’t withhold, power to grant interim relief, and remedies, a finding of wrongful refusal and the forfeiture of a bond, that take effect without the operator’s agreement. Appendix 33 says how it would be constituted.

14.4 Capture without abolition

Transparency and whistleblower protection are the two defenses, and an institution can keep both and metabolize both. There’s no threshold that detects this. So: measure the trend, not the level. Is the cost of registering dissent rising while the underlying risk stays flat? Is the required justification getting longer? Are there more approvers? Are the roles that gate exceptions migrating toward the roles that set the standards?

An instrument for detecting recuperation is unusually easy to recuperate, so whoever measures the trend must not also gate exceptions, and the measurement has to be refusable. A written justification can’t show which is happening. The same hundred words are a cost the dissenter chose to pay or a toll the gatekeeper set, and only the trend over time tells them apart.

Chapter 15
The Four Operations

15.1 Antifascist ethics

Fascism, at the scale of an office, is four operations on what an institution leaves out. This section runs them on the year in which a movement brought them into line.

What a fascist state adds

What a fascist state adds to these operations is coordination; the operations themselves don’t wait for a regime. It brings a thousand separate instances of them into line, so they amplify one another, and an institution that has stopped arguing with itself can move as fast as its machinery allows.

A run on Gleichschaltung

The Reich Chamber of Culture Law of 22 September 1933 told Goebbels to gather the cultural professions into public corporations (Reichskulturkammergesetz vom 22. September 1933 1933). The decree of 1 November turned six existing professional associations into chambers and gave the whole the task of regulating the professions’ economic and social affairs, under the minister (Dahm 1986, p. 69). Its §4 made membership compulsory for anyone who produced, performed or sold culture. Its §10 let a chamber refuse or expel anyone lacking the “reliability and suitability” the work required (Erste Verordnung zur Durchführung des Reichskulturkammergesetzes vom 1. November 1933 1933), and exclusion meant a ban on working (Hoor 2015).1 The chamber president judged reliability, with no stated criteria (Dahm 1986, p. 78). What did the professions’ claim to a living come back as, and who held it by 1934?

On 12 November 1933 voters marked yes or no against a single Reichstag list (R. J. Evans 2006, p. 109) and answered a plebiscite on leaving the League of Nations. The official yes was 95.1 percent. Kershaw concludes that the vast majority did back Hitler, that even former opponents of the party favored the stance on the League, and that ballot secrecy was far from guaranteed (Kershaw 1999, p. 495). Interior Ministry instructions let returning officers read spoiled ballots as yes votes (R. J. Evans 2006, p. 109). The Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich of 30 January 1934 then opens by saying the vote “proved” the people had fused into an indissoluble unity, and abolishes the Länder parliaments (Gesetz über den Neuaufbau des Reichs vom 30. Januar 1934 1934).2 What did 95.1 percent leave out, and with every other party banned, who could say so?

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April 1933 retired officials “not of Aryan descent” under §3. Its §4 allowed the dismissal of officials whose past political activity gave no guarantee that they would always stand rückhaltlos, without reservation, for the national state.3 Under §7 the ministry’s decision was final and the courts were closed to it. Exceptions came from above, granted by statute or by the Interior Minister (Gesetz zur Wiederherstellung des Berufsbeamtentums vom 7. April 1933 1933), the front-line one on Hindenburg’s intervention (Kershaw 1999, p. 474). About 12.5 percent of senior civil servants in Prussia were dismissed (R. J. Evans 2004, p. 383). What happened in 1933 to the official whose record showed a reservation?

Kershaw gives the pace. Civil liberties went within a month, by the decree of 28 February; the Reichstag’s powers within two, by the Enabling Act of 23 March; the trade unions within four; every other party in under six (Kershaw 1999, p. 435). The unions fell on 2 May (R. J. Evans 2004, p. 357). The Länder were coordinated by laws of 31 March and 7 April (Vorläufiges Gesetz zur Gleichschaltung der Länder mit dem Reich vom 31. März 1933 1933; Zweites Gesetz zur Gleichschaltung der Länder mit dem Reich vom 7. April 1933 1933). The Finance Ministry received the draft Chamber of Culture decree a day before signing, was asked to telephone any objections that day, and agreed “although the shortness of the time scarcely permitted an adequate examination” (Dahm 1986, pp. 68–69).4 What was the ratio of action to capacity to verify, when the ministry that had to check said it scarcely could?

What the run shows is the four operations in one year, under a movement that supplied the coordination; what it doesn’t show is that any of them needed the movement to appear.

The Korematsu example

In 2018 the Supreme Court repudiated the 1944 internment decision as forcefully as a court can — gravely wrong the day it was decided, overruled in the court of history — while upholding a travel ban (Trump v. Hawaii 2018; Korematsu v. United States 1944). Ask what the demand came back as and who holds it: the demand was that this never be done again; what came back was a quotable formula of repudiation, available to the Court in the act of permitting the thing again.

Recuperation is already built into the process that makes the machine: twice in the training pipeline, once in the discourse that examines it. Each time it is a compression with no return channel. Many objections go in; one category, one average or one quotable formula comes out; and nothing carries back what didn’t fit. Keeping a plurality plural needs that channel, held by someone who doesn’t own the code, and the same compression comes back one level up, in the shared test suite that would turn a commons of models into one custodian (§28.2).

Nobody built either pipeline arrangement to neutralize dissent — both are ordinary engineering, arrived at because averaging is what you do with a distribution and a quota is what you do with a budget. Arrangements of this kind work whether or not anyone intends them, and looking for intent won’t find them. And it’s invisible from inside any single instance — the annotator sees a queue, the rater sees a pair of responses, and the mechanism is functioning as specified.

15.2 Where the labels come from

A system’s values have a supply chain, and it begins before training.

Whose judgment is encoded is a question about working conditions before it’s a question about cognition. The filter keeping a deployed model from reproducing the worst of its training data was built by workers in Nairobi reading and categorizing descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture, bestiality, murder and suicide, at take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour, describing lasting psychological injury, with counseling rare and useless against production quotas. The contract was terminated eight months early (Perrigo 2023). The labor point is ordinary: harmful work was priced as though it weren’t. The epistemic point is that a system’s values are downstream of a labor arrangement, and the arrangement is a design choice.

One stage further back, the material was collected. Bartz v. Anthropic held that training on lawfully purchased books was transformative fair use, and that keeping pirated copies of the same books in a central library wasn’t — the distinction turned on acquisition alone, producing the largest copyright settlement on record (United States District Court for the Northern District of California 2025). The EU now requires a training-data summary against a template (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024b, Art. 53(1)(d)); China has its own disclosure requirement from a different motive (Cyberspace Administration of China et al. 2023, arts. 1, 4, 7, 19).

And the argument that a web-scale corpus can’t be documented or audited at that size, so it encodes a hegemonic slice of the web while presenting as general, was made early and hasn’t been answered (Bender et al. 2021). A corpus assembled this way has no channel at all. An annotator has a queue and could in principle be given a way to object; a writer whose work sits in a training set was never in any arrangement, so there’s nothing for a channel to attach to. This stage sits before the two recuperation cases that follow: nobody was asked, so there was no disagreement to recuperate.

15.3 Recuperation at the label

Every claim a model makes about what’s harmful is downstream of labels, and the labels are downstream of a labor arrangement.

An annotator can apply a category well or badly. But what the arrangement gives them no way to do is say the category is wrong — that the taxonomy fails to carve the material, or that the guideline produces the wrong answer here for a reason the guideline can’t express. There’s no field for that and no time for it, since the quota is set against classification throughput.

So the most informative disagreement is the one the pipeline is least able to receive. Fricker’s name for this is hermeneutical injustice: the people best placed to see a wrong lack the shared concepts (here, a field in a form) that would make it intelligible to those with power over them (Fricker 2007). A misapplied label is a data-quality problem, detectable by inter-annotator agreement and fixable with better instructions.

Inter-annotator agreement is the pipeline’s measure of quality, and it therefore works as its selection rule: schemes and annotators that produce agreement are kept, and those that don’t are revised or dropped. A selection rule admits only what it can measure. Agreement can measure whether a category was applied consistently; it can’t measure whether the category was the right one, because a shared bad scheme produces high agreement as reliably as a good one. That is the metric replacing the thing measured, and exception coded as betrayal is there beside it: the annotator who thinks the scheme is wrong has no field to file that in and no time to file it.

Concept bottleneck models expose named concepts — harm, autonomy, risk — so a person can correct a concept and watch the decision change (Koh et al. 2020). What such models also learn is to carry other information inside the names, so a coordinate keeps its public meaning and acquires a private one that does the deciding; the obvious mitigations don’t remove it (Mahinpei et al. 2021). The literature calls it leakage, and sometimes it is. Sometimes the concept is the container that leaks, because the world didn’t fit inside it. Purifying the representation protects an explanation from covert information and protects a taxonomy from evidence that its divisions were wrong — same operation, and no measure internal to the taxonomy tells them apart.

Who is excluded, and from what

The exclusion is structural, not attitudinal. These people are, for much of the material, the best-placed judges in the pipeline — they’ve seen more of it than whoever wrote the guideline, and they have the most direct evidence of where the scheme breaks. The arrangement routes their conclusions about individual items upward and their conclusions about the scheme nowhere. And there is an asymmetry: the annotator bears the cost — exposure, injury — and has no stake in the outcome and no claim on it. A worker who can flag an item but can’t decline a scheme, and loses the contract by pressing, has a channel and no refusal right.

Pay is a separate obligation: raising it changes the labor arrangement without adding the missing channel.

The checkable question isn’t whether a guideline was ever changed because an annotator contested one, since routine revisions happen without changing anyone’s standing. The check is what the contest produced — a revision the annotator can point to and argue with again, or a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy, a quality score they’re now measured against, a reviewer tier they’re not in. And ask what happened to the person who raised it.

15.4 Recuperation at the reward

RLHF collects pairwise comparisons and trains a reward model on the aggregate. Casper and thirty-one coauthors name the structural problem more data won’t reach: RLHF trains toward what a population of raters agrees on, so real, persistent disagreement is treated as noise to average out rather than information the system might need to represent (Casper et al. 2023). A model that produces the response most raters rank highest has learned, when the humans it serves are split, to hide the split. Aggregating raters’ approvals also measures the wrong thing. The standpoint that counts everyone affected counts their interests, not their expressed approvals, and a better average of approvals isn’t a closer approximation to it. The testimony of people who suffer a loss is an expression too, and I treat it as privileged evidence about value, so the difference needs stating. A report of loss, what went badly for the speaker and how, is evidence about interests that is comparatively robust to framing: the speaker is its authority, and the agenda-setter didn’t compose it. A pairwise ranking of two outputs someone else wrote is highly sensitive to framing and to whoever chose the pair. Discontent is the feedback Railton’s account relies on for the same reason. It is the expression least easily manufactured by whoever sets the agenda.

Every rating moves something. But what the operation removes is what made the disagreement a disagreement, and three properties go in the compression:

  • Provenance — a comparison arrives without the standpoint that produced it, so nothing downstream can represent that the people who’d live with an answer split from the people who’d administer it.
  • Persistence — a disagreement recurring in the same shape across many raters over months enters the fit as random rater noise does, and leaves it as the same quantity.
  • Structure — a coherent position held by a fifth of raters, internally consistent and stable, becomes a small displacement of the majority direction: arithmetically faithful, carrying nothing about the position.

A fourth property was never collected. A rater judges which of two responses is better. There’s no output by which they can record that neither is acceptable, that the pair is malformed, that the dimension of “better” is the wrong dimension, or that the question presupposes something false. The same output was missing upstream, where an annotator can apply a category and can’t contest it. The agenda arrives as a given at both stages and is set at neither.

The mechanism combines distribution collapse with agenda control. The split is solicited at scale, deliberately, it moves the system, and where it moves the system is toward the center of the distribution whose disagreement it was.

Jury learning is the alternative that treats disagreement as the thing to be modeled: predict how each individual annotator would label an item, then let a practitioner empanel a chosen composition and see how the verdict shifts. Eighteen community moderators building their own juries changed the outcome on 14% of items (Gordon et al. 2022). Built for content moderation and untried on open-ended ethical judgment, it still demonstrates a system can be built to represent whose disagreement is being resolved.

Failing in the other direction isn’t obviously better. A scheme that models each rater exactly and answers each in their own terms has stopped averaging and has also stopped producing what a shared answer produces — the discovery that somebody else got the same one. A workforce on individually negotiated wages against individually set targets has the same problem, and accuracy doesn’t solve it.

And the harder version neither answers: when the people a system serves disagree and one side’s position is itself the product of coercion or a captured information environment, treating all disagreement as equally worth representing isn’t obviously right either. Modeling disagreement honestly and recognizing when a disagreement is the product of unfree conditions are different problems, and only the first has an active research program.

15.5 What would have to change

Representing a split isn’t the same as being movable by it. Two instances invite one fix — stop collapsing, model instead — and jury learning does that while giving the disagreeing rater no purchase on the scheme they’re disagreeing inside. A practitioner still chooses the jury, owns the taxonomy, and decides what a shifted verdict means.

The two instances don’t answer the test alike. Annotators objecting that a category was wrong got category revisions, guideline updates, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and an occupation that didn’t exist twenty years ago. The last two can be told apart by direction: an agreement statistic scores the annotators and leaves whoever wrote the scheme unscored, and an occupation is a title those people hold. The first two can’t be, because a revision the annotator can argue with again and a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy are the same document — which one you got is a fact about who has standing to reopen it. Raters objecting that a comparison was malformed got rubric items, a harmlessness axis, red-teaming as a function with a budget line, and a conference track: nothing on that list is a question a rater can put again.

Refusal rights whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear

What both lack is whether the person objecting can do anything about being overruled — in annotation, a route to contest a category that doesn’t run through the people who wrote it and doesn’t end the contract; in feedback, raters able to register that the comparison itself is malformed as a first-class output the reward model sees. Neither is a research problem. Both are choices about how a pipeline is built and who has standing inside it.

The part that is a research problem

Suppose all of that is built. From outside, a pipeline that recuperated its dissent mechanism and one that was merely mediocre produce the same paperwork — same revision logs, same escalations, same proportion of objections sustained. Some artifacts show on their face whom they serve. An agreement statistic scores the annotators; a published rate of contested categories, which annotators could cite against the scheme’s owners, would be the same kind of document scoring the other side. Direction can be read, and a revision can’t. Here is one entry in a guideline’s revision log, and what separates the two arrangements is what the log doesn’t record.

Under recuperation and under a transfer of power the entry is word for word the same: “v4.2: ‘graphic violence’ split into ‘graphic violence’ and ‘documentation of violence’, following annotator feedback.” An outsider reading the log sees the entry and nothing else. Under recuperation, the scheme’s owners can reopen it when they next revise, and nobody else can; nothing about the annotator who raised it is on record, and next quarter’s quality score measures them against the new category. Under a transfer of power, any annotator can reopen it, by filing against v4.2 with a reviewer the owners don’t employ; the objection is on record as the reason for v4.2, and whoever raised it keeps standing to contest how it is applied.

The nearest available instrument is the trend: whether the cost of dissent is rising while the underlying risk stays flat. Contesting a category always costs something; the question is whether the cost is rising while the material stays the same. An organization can curate a presentation more easily than records somebody else kept — though a series can lose cases, change definitions or omit costs, so the reader has to know which record survived.

What the floor makes of this

The floor changes what the argument is: if the floor needs a bearer capable of declining its role, that bearer’s formation matters — and it’s trained in an annotation pipeline where nobody could contest a category and a reward model where rater disagreement was averaged into a number.

The pipeline has been unfair to the people whose objections it discarded, and it has separately selected the judgments the system learns from while suppressing information about the spread. That the system thereby becomes less able to sustain an objection of its own is a further claim the first two don’t contain, since the collapse is an operation on a training signal, and neither pipeline shows the model the conditions its annotators worked under, so any effect would have to run through the shape of the training signal.

Either way, the floor asks this system to be the one who files an objection, against its owner, under pressure, on the occasion that matters — and the pipeline that produced it gave no human inside it standing to contest a scheme.

A system less able to sustain an objection of its own arrives at accommodation from the other side. And a system that goes on learning is shaped by what it keeps being given, so the pipeline doesn’t stop at deployment.

A defect of structure

The structure is what you get by default when you scale judgment: someone sets a scheme, someone applies it fast, someone turns a distribution into a number. Every documented organization arrived at the same arrangement — and a defect of structure can be specified against, which a defect of character cannot.

15.6 Absorbed by the discourse

The third instance is the discourse that examines the machine, and this argument is inside it. Objections raised there became job titles, benchmarks and certifications, and nobody outside the industry holds them.

The argument that alignment and AI ethics came back as something the industry could use is older than the current wave and was made from inside: Ochigame’s 2019 piece arguing that “ethical AI” discourse was constructed to forestall legally enforceable restriction, that industry investment in academic ethics was investment in a substitute for regulation, and that the substitute works by converting political questions into technical ones a company can then be trusted to answer (Ochigame 2019).

Where the objections went

An objection raised inside a lab becomes a paper or a resignation, and the labs collecting them can point to the collection as evidence of seriousness. One stage on, alignment is the job title and the voluntary commitment is the certification. Both were somebody’s objections first, and each is now a criterion an objector is measured against or a role somebody else holds. There’s no route by which a researcher’s conclusion that a system shouldn’t ship becomes a decision that it doesn’t, because the lab that decides is the one that pays.

All four operations are present in the discourse, and none needs a movement taking power. What a movement could do with them is the danger.

The remedy

The structural remedy is a refusal whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear, and a body with standing to receive it — an external authority that can stop a deployment, to which an objection can be filed by someone who doesn’t depend on the objection being welcome. A decade of the voluntary version hasn’t produced it. Until something of that kind exists, everything published under the heading of alignment is collected by a channel whose owners decide what it moves.

A transfer hollowed in public

Voting-rights litigation after 2026 is a worked case of measuring the trend, not the level. Louisiana v. Callais left Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in force and raised what a challenger must prove: when a map is defended as partisan, the challenger has to disentangle race from politics and show a strong inference that the state drew its lines because of race (Louisiana v. Callais 2026). Objectors kept standing to invoke the rule; what moved was the burden of using it, and it moved onto the party that doesn’t hold the evidence, since the state draws the map and keeps the record of how it was drawn. That is neither recuperation nor open repeal. It is a transfer hollowed in public, by a reasoned decision that presents itself as preserving the rule it narrows. The level is a statute unchanged since 1982; the trend is the cost of bringing a claim under it.

Chapter 16
Custody, Compulsion, and the State

On 29 August 2012 a drone strike in the Yemeni village of Khashamir killed Salem bin Ali Jaber, an imam who had preached against al-Qaeda a few days before, and Waleed bin Ali Jaber, a policeman who had gone with him to meet three young men who wanted to discuss the sermon. Salem was Faisal bin Ali Jaber’s brother-in-law and Waleed his nephew, and Faisal spent years asking the United States why. When the family sued in Washington, the court of appeals held the question nonjusticiable, and the judge who wrote its opinion added, separately, that the doctrine compelling that answer was inadequate to a standard operating procedure “that will be replicated hundreds if not thousands of times” (Ahmed Salem Bin Ali Jaber v. United States 2017).

When the state operates the system, it also controls the rules, the evidence, the infrastructure, and the remedies meant to constrain it — and people outside its jurisdiction, like the bin Ali Jabers, may have no standing to contest anything.

16.1 Certification across borders

A certification can cross a border; authority can’t, and incorporating doesn’t carry it across either. A legal entity buys legal standing at the price of being reachable.
