A network incorporated under one state’s statute gains a name, an agent and a docket number, and becomes something that state’s courts and the federal courts can reach. An entity that can be named in a licence can be named in an order. Whatever gives a floor something to bind (a name, an agent, assets, a docket number) gives a state something to compel. A certificate says a system was tested against a stated process, or that one regulator accepts another’s finding. None of that establishes that whoever selected the floor was entitled to select it for the people subject to the deployment — and the question reopens wherever the system goes. Local adaptation doesn’t resolve it, because adaptation is another chance to amend the floor. Adjustments chosen by the operating government and adjustments chosen by the people subject to the system can produce identical technical documentation and carry opposite claims to legitimacy. International governance matters here only when it assigns somebody access to evidence, authority to compel a change, or power to stop a deployment against the operator’s wishes.

16.2 Where the state’s leverage sits

Not in national AI strategies but in physical and legal chokepoints: chips, fabrication equipment, electricity, water, land-use permits, procurement contracts, and the jurisdiction a developer is incorporated in. The same leverage that lets a government enforce a floor lets it remove one. An inspection body can be independent of the operator and still depend on a licence or appropriation controlled by the state it’s inspecting. A company may resist a customer and be unable to resist its home government. So the custody question moves outward: who controls the conditions under which the model, its operator, and its reviewer are allowed to keep operating.

A chip also has to be installed, powered and cooled, which lands on grids, water systems and zoning authorities on a timescale of years. That hands a state leverage needing no export-control regime at all — an interconnection queue, a water allocation, a permit. Much of a government’s actual leverage is exercised by permitting authorities that weren’t designed with AI in mind and don’t think of themselves as regulators of it. Those authorities are therefore the ones actually deciding whether the capacity exists, and a polity that can constrain where a datacenter is built and never what it’s used for has been handed the silent failure of a floor drawn too narrowly.

A model runs on a machine, the machine sits in a building, the building draws power and water and returns heat and exhaust — the part an audit of outputs cannot see. Where those buildings go is decided on land price, power price and permit speed, which is also a description of the places least able to refuse one. Datacenters used around 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, roughly 1.5% of world consumption. Their demand is growing about 12% a year, four times as fast as electricity demand overall, and is projected near 945 TWh by 2030 (International Energy Agency 2025). Google reports that 87% of its freshwater withdrawal came from low- or medium-risk sources, the company’s own way of recording where the rest came from (Google LLC 2026). And the NAACP has sued over 27 gas turbines near Memphis run without an air permit near homes, schools and churches, claiming more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP 2026). The benefit is realized wherever the model is sold; the cost is concentrated within a few miles of those turbines, among people who took no part in the transaction. A system can be perfectly calibrated across every demographic its outputs touch and still have been assembled this way, because nothing in the model’s behavior records where its costs were placed.

The people within a few miles of the turbines are acted on by the deployment and had no standing to contest it. The remedy isn’t a floor term. It is a siting and permitting rule, and it belongs here, with the state’s other chokepoints.

The capacity is dual by construction: the concentration that makes a targeting pipeline possible was built and justified on consumer terms, and nothing in the buildout separates the two. A targeting cell, a border screening queue and a surveillance program are separate institutions, and a shared substrate brings them into line without anyone building it to. And the dependence is a point of control: a government that can permit, regulate or close the infrastructure has leverage over whoever owns it.

The competitive framing has a cost: a government racing to field a capability has a structural reason to defer the question of how it gets used and against whom. Turned inward, the same infrastructure is biometric surveillance and automated censorship — requiring no different technology, only a government willing to point it at its own population and nothing stopping it. And states aren’t the only actors anymore: the dollar cost of the largest training runs has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016, as labs have made those runs larger, even while the cost of each unit of computing has fallen (Cottier et al. 2024), putting frontier development inside a handful of well-capitalized companies, so a government’s real leverage over “its” national capability depends on how much of it sits in companies it can regulate, tax or requisition, and how much sits in companies it can only ask.

16.3 Custody and state compulsion

A government needn’t alter a model to defeat a constraint; it can compel whoever holds it. The Apple case tested that in about as protected a jurisdiction as exists: a magistrate ordered Apple under the All Writs Act to write and sign software defeating passcode protections on a phone (In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone Seized During the Execution of a Search Warrant on a Black Lexus IS300, California License Plate 35KGD203 2016). Apple refused and moved to vacate, arguing the authority wouldn’t stop at one phone. The question was never decided — the FBI found a third party and withdrew. So whether a democracy with an independent judiciary can force an unwilling company to compromise a system it built is legally untested. A government doesn’t need that argument to lean on a vendor. The 2026 vendor dispute is the case: a vendor that refused to permit fully autonomous targeting and mass domestic surveillance was threatened with contract termination and designated a supply-chain risk. China’s 2023 generative-AI rules exercise the same leverage as a standing condition of operating (Cyberspace Administration of China et al. 2023, arts. 4, 14, 17, 19, 21). One government compelled case by case, against a vendor that refused, and the courts divided by statute, one setting aside the designation as retaliation and the other upholding a separate exclusion as turning on the refused contract term; the other compels in advance, as a term of doing business.

The American instrument that compels in advance is older than either case. Under Title I of the Defense Production Act the government places a rated order, which a supplier that normally makes the item must accept and fill ahead of other work; the grounds for rejecting one are narrow, objection to the use is not among them, and refusal carries a statutory penalty with no court in between (Defense Production Act of 1950 1950; Defense Priorities and Allocations System 2026). A rated order says nothing about use. It compels delivery, and whether what the government does with the delivery is lawful stays the law of armed conflict’s question, which leaves the vendor in the responsibility gap with the supply compelled. Two things follow. A vendor’s refusal of a rated order is a refusal of a federal order at a price fixed in advance, which is the form that counts, and it is the form the 2026 dispute would have taken had the government carried out its threat to invoke the older statute (Amodei 2026). And a rated order gets the vendor’s product. If the product holds the floor, the order gets a floored model, and compelling the vendor to remove the floor is compelling it to write code it doesn’t want to write, which is the Apple question again, one step later and as untested.

Custody can be distributed without disappearing. Published weights can’t be recalled by an order aimed at the developer; maintainers across jurisdictions raise the cost. None of that removes the leverage — a developer with employees, offices and legal existence inside a border answers to that government’s courts regardless of how the model is built, and no architectural choice changes who can be held in contempt. Nobody has tested that leverage against a model built specifically to resist the government making the request.

16.4 Military custody and the responsibility gap

In Gaza, the approval stage supplied authorization without judgment. In Maven, the vendor supplies the infrastructure making unprecedented throughput possible while locating responsibility entirely within the military organization. At machine tempo the reviewer can be treated as a component, the supplier can stand outside the decision, and the institution can remain responsible only in the abstract.

Military custody is where the chapter’s problem is most acute: the operator is the sovereign that can compel the institutions meant to constrain it — classify the evidence, define the reviewer’s jurisdiction, terminate a contract, restrict a supplier, and decide whether an adverse finding reaches anyone able to stop the operation.

A targeting decision passes through more parties than the chain of command names: the commander who authorizes, the operator who uses, the contractor who integrates (whose embedded personnel may sit close enough to the targeting cell that “effectively acting as a commander” is a real question), the commercial vendor whose model supplies part of the capability and whose personnel are nowhere near it, and the system producing the output. The questions that matter are which of them could have known how the system was used, which had authority to refuse or stop it, and which can be made to answer afterward.

The American domestic rule most concerned with human judgment, DoD Directive 3000.09, requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems to allow “appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force” (U.S. Department of Defense 2023). A system that generates and ranks targets without firing anything is decision support, which plausibly falls outside it. Maven sits in that gap: the domestic rule written for human judgment doesn’t cover the system that compressed it.

Article 28 of the Rome Statute (International Criminal Court 1998) is the doctrine built for the case where the person who authorized an act didn’t perform it — a commander is responsible for crimes by forces under effective control where they knew or should have known and failed to take necessary measures. Neither branch asks what a subordinate intended. But the Court’s jurisdiction runs to natural persons, and the provision presupposes forces that can commit a crime and be disciplined — a targeting system is an instrument. So the question is whether the human elements can still be proved once the instrument is doing the work.

The fourth party no doctrine covers

The operator, the command and the weapon’s developer are all inside the military. The model’s developer isn’t. Command responsibility doesn’t extend to the vendor — not because it sits outside a chain of command (Article 28’s civilian branch was written for superiors with no chain of command) but because nobody at the company has effective authority over the military personnel who commit the underlying crime, and an airstrike isn’t an activity within any vendor employee’s effective responsibility. A use policy, a licensing term, a right to refuse service, even a technical cut-off are not that relationship. Individual liability under Article 25 stays available in principle with demanding mental elements — facilitation requires acting for the purpose of facilitating — and ordinary supply of a general-purpose model approaches neither.

Product liability is the other half and it’s untested, with two obstacles: the model isn’t defective in the sense the doctrine most readily covers, and a sophisticated intermediary chose the application. Where the doctrine has been rewritten for software it moved away from this case, as the EU’s directive shows below. Untested isn’t exempt, but no vendor is currently answering to it. The vendor sits in a gap nobody designed, produced by applying to it two bodies of law written for soldiers and for manufacturers.

There is also a jurisdictional gap alongside the doctrinal one: ICC jurisdiction is territorial or by nationality, so one of the two campaigns here sits inside a live instrument and the other sits outside it.

“I do not know whether my system was used.”

Matthias’s responsibility gap is control distributed until nobody holds enough of it to answer (Matthias 2004) — a gap in causal control. What the model developer’s case exhibits is different and more tractable: a gap in causal visibility. Asked about his company’s models and Minab, Anthropic’s chief executive said, “we don’t know exactly how these models were used” (Stan 2026). Take the answer as true. The question is how an arrangement was built in which it could be true.

The paperwork for four July 2025 frontier-model agreements, released in August 2026 under a Freedom of Information Act suit (Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology 2026; Biddle 2026), shows something more exact than an absence of oversight terms. One amended agreement carries a section headed System Oversight, withheld in full; the released documents for two of the other three carry no such section at all.

And whether a developer reserved an inspection right matters little. A right exercised inside an accredited classified environment produces findings classified with it. Public accountability needs a body that can initiate scrutiny without belonging to the state and say afterwards what it found. No commercial term supplies that, and the redaction is the demonstration: whatever the withheld section says, the people the deployment is aimed at can’t read it.

Matthias’s gap may not be closable, but absent visibility is an instrumentation choice: logging is solved, contractual inspection rights are ordinary, and a vendor that wanted to know could require, as a condition of licensing into a targeting platform, that categories of use be recorded and made available to a named auditor.

The government’s own acquisition guidance is the better evidence, because it’s complete. OMB’s April 2025 memorandum lists what agencies should secure from vendors, from data rights and portability to pricing transparency, and every item runs from the vendor to the government; none runs back (U.S. Office of Management and Budget 2025). The contracting vehicle explains the absence. The four agreements were other transactions, which carry no FAR provisions by default, so a contracting officer decides case by case which protections to write in, and GAO has found these instruments risk reduced accountability and transparency (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2026a). A System Oversight section can be missing without anyone having removed it.

The pressure that matters is the advantage attached to removing judgment from the timeline. If one state fields systems that act faster because nobody can intervene before engagement, competitors acquire a reason to match the speed and give up the check. “Meaningful human control” stays true as a description of formal authority while becoming false as a description of what anyone can do before the system acts. And the pressure reaches the reviewers: a military treating delay as operational risk has reason to narrow what requires clearance and move review from authorization-before to explanation-after. Nothing has formally abolished oversight; it has been moved to after the act. So the enforceable question is who can slow or suspend the system without first getting permission from the command whose advantage depends on keeping it fast.

16.5 Classification as a custody problem

Classification does three things to a refusal, and this section collects them. It keeps the reason from the refuser: the case description is the only channel, and Minab stays coded as it was (position 3). It keeps the record from the public: an investigation officials call complete and not released, a System Oversight section withheld in full, a review ratio no outsider can read. And it keeps the reviewer from being adverse: a cleared committee’s lever is a budget line, an inspector general sits inside, and the people a deployment is aimed at can’t be cleared into their own case.1 Three kinds of secrecy produce these effects. Essential secrecy, where the operation fails if the enemy can read it. Accidental secrecy, where a default classifies what nobody decided to keep. And evasive secrecy, where review is moved from authorization-before to explanation-after by classifying the evidence it would need. My instruments answer them differently, and this section says which answers which.

Essential secrecy is answered by letting evidence in, not out. Classification stops information leaving, and bringing it in is routine, so the import condition, deconfliction coordinates and open-source imagery brought into the enclave as a condition of licensing, puts evidence the operator didn’t compose where the system can reach it without anything leaving. A refuser inside the compartment works as a cleared bearer does, and the operation’s secrets stay where they were.

Accidental secrecy is answered by the record. The review ratio and the committed log are lodged with an adverse party when the act occurs and published after the campaign, and class-level notice publishes the classes and counts on the same lag, so what nobody decided to keep secret comes out on a schedule nobody has to decide.

Evasive secrecy is the hard case, because there the classification is the act. It is answered by an adverse party with standing: counsel for the people a deployment affects, cleared and appearing as of right; the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already supplies in criminal cases; and the trend measure, which shows whether what dissent costs is rising while the risk stays flat.

16.6 Where liability extends, and where it stops

One of the two bodies of law has now been rewritten for software, and what it covers fits in a sentence: a duty to disclose evidence, and a presumption against the party withholding it, in force where the harm is physical and the defendant is a manufacturer. Those two conditions exclude the cases I have described.

The EU’s recast product liability directive (applying from December 2026) makes economic operators liable without fault and carries the instrument built for opacity — a court can order disclosure, and where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult it may presume defect and causation once the claimant shows each is likely (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024a). A mechanism designed for a system nobody outside can inspect is already law. Two features fix how far it travels: the defendant is that economic operator, not a state deploying what it bought; and the damage is a closed list — death or personal injury including medically recognised psychological harm, property damage, and corruption of non-professional data. The first is wider than it sounds and is where these cases enter if they enter at all: a discriminatory score or an unappealable refusal is recoverable once it has made somebody ill, and not before. The wrong itself, and the economic loss following it, is outside the list.

The proposal that would have covered those was withdrawn — the 2022 AI Liability Directive would have added a fault-based route with the same presumption, beyond defect and beyond the damage list. Member states and industry couldn’t agree; it was announced for withdrawal in February 2025 and withdrawn that October (European Commission 2022). Outside the enacted directive, what remains is Matthias’s gap governed by whatever national law says about a case none of it was written for. And a compensation regime of either kind answers one of the four gaps Santoni de Sio and Mecacci distinguish (Sio and Mecacci 2021) — culpability. Moral accountability, public accountability, and the duty to prevent a harm before it occurs are untouched.

The electronic personhood debate approached the gap from the other side, asking whether the system itself could answer. The European Parliament’s 2017 resolution floated a status for the most autonomous systems (European Parliament 2017); in an open letter the following year, 150+ researchers and legal scholars objected that personhood for a system with no consciousness would let a manufacturer offload liability onto a fiction with no assets (Open Letter to the European Commission 2018). Giving a bearer assets answers the second half of that objection and not the first. Responsibility follows causal control: the builder answers for how it trained the thing, the operator for what it demanded, the bearer for what it decided knowing what it knew — and no arrangement of accounts moves a design decision away from whoever made it.

Apportioning causal contribution across a training pipeline after a harm has no method, and until it does the apportionment is drafted. Two drafts exist: one enacted and confined to defect, one negotiated, withdrawn, and left on the record with its terms intact. Neither was rejected as unworkable, and the second’s terms are available to whoever drafts the next one. The nearest proposal aimed at these cases is Crootof’s war torts: state liability for civilian harms caused in armed conflict, whether or not anyone committed a war crime (Crootof 2016; Crootof 2022). It covers the state as operator, which the product directive doesn’t, and it needs a forum, which the floor court would supply.

Beyond the directive’s limits a reviewer can be granted access, publish what it finds, and have produced nothing anybody must act on until somebody is answerable for it.

16.7 Who can bind the state that enforces the rule?

A state can bind a private developer because it controls something the developer needs. When the state is the operator, the institution that writes the rule, controls the evidence and supplies the remedy is the institution the rule is meant to constrain.

Standing to sue has never turned on citizenship, and the doctrines closing American courts to targeting claims — political question, collapsed damages remedies, state secrets, statutory exceptions for injuries abroad and combatant activities — are indifferent to who the plaintiff is. They close the forum for a subject matter, and they’ve closed it to citizens. Three Americans killed in Yemen in 2011, one a sixteen-year-old nobody alleges was targeted: the court held that a plausible due-process claim had been stated as to the one who was targeted, and that no remedy was available for it (Al-Aulaqi v. Panetta 2014). A separate suit by an American journalist who survived five drone strikes was dismissed for want of standing to sue after a state-secrets dismissal below (Kareem v. Haspel 2021).

And those cases concentrate in one appellate circuit by venue and by where the defendants sit — so the ordinary correction mechanism, several circuits disagreeing and forcing a higher court’s attention, doesn’t run. The doctrine hardens without ever being tested against a competing reading.

The mechanisms can work as mechanisms and fail as checks. In the Israeli case the apparatus performed — journalists published, serving personnel spoke, the courts were trying a sitting prime minister. No finding attached to a body with standing to stop what it described.

The American version: a civilian-harm investigation into Minab was, by officials’ account, effectively complete for months and not released, while a Pentagon spokesperson said it remained ongoing (Bartenstein and Karra 2026; Shrivastav 2026) — and the lever available to the Senate committee was withholding three-quarters of the Defense Secretary’s travel budget until the unredacted investigation was handed over (Stassis 2026).

What the Pentagon wouldn’t publish, the UN mission did. The finding is public, reasoned, and attached to nothing — no jurisdiction, no answer to the mission’s requests for information (Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran 2026, para. 97) and none to its findings beyond a statement that engaged none of the evidence (Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty 2026), the domestic investigation still unreleased.

The courts show the same pattern: transparency litigation succeeded where damages litigation failed. A court of appeals compelled disclosure of the executive’s own legal analysis of targeted killing (New York Times Co. v. United States Department of Justice 2014). The judiciary will make a government explain the legal basis on which it killed somebody and will not decide whether the killing was lawful.

What matters here is rules binding a state toward people who’ll never vote in its elections, the purpose of international humanitarian law; what it hasn’t supplied is a forum, and the bin Ali Jabers’ case shows the forum switched off at home as well, by a decision that never had to reach who was suing.

All but one of the forum closures above are Congress’s to change. A statute can create a cause of action for people harmed by a deployment that crossed its floor; waive sovereign immunity for it, including the Federal Tort Claims Act’s exceptions for combatant activities and for claims arising abroad (United States Congress 1946); and replace dismissal on state-secrets grounds with the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already uses in criminal cases, in which a judge reviews the evidence, the case goes on, and a government that still withholds evidence bears the cost (United States Congress 1980). None of that needs a new court, and a new court without it would reproduce al-Aulaqi: a plausible claim and no remedy. Under capture, a refusal’s remaining work is a record, and a record matters only if it can reach whoever made the decision. Under Trump v. United States (Trump v. United States 2024), the President is absolutely immune for acts within his core constitutional powers and at least presumptively immune for his other official acts, commanding the armed forces among them, and testimony or records probing immune conduct can’t be put before a jury. So the record reaches every commander except the one at the top, and a statute saying otherwise would be reviewed by the Court that made the holding. Making the record reach him means changing the Court. Appendix 33 sets out a program for that.

The chapter’s cases are American, and “the state” is tested here on one constitutional order. Europe is a different one: the Convention applies, has extraterritorial reach, and produces judgments states sometimes obey; there is no state-secrets privilege of the American kind and no collapsed damages remedy. The AI Act makes the boundary visible: it can require documentation from private providers, subject high-risk systems to review, and impose penalties tied to global turnover — and it excludes military, defence and national-security uses from its scope. Public authorities stay covered elsewhere, but enforcement against a member state’s agencies still runs through institutions that state constitutes.

For review to bind here, the chain that makes review binding has to run against a state: initiation by people outside its electorate, evidence it would withhold, an interim order before the use is complete, and a remedy that doesn’t need its consent. A principle supplying none of those may state the rule correctly and identifies nobody who can make the state obey it.

A treaty obligation of that kind exists: the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention, binding at the level of a human-rights instrument with operational detail left to domestic law (Council of Europe 2024) — and not yet in force, needing five ratifications, of which the EU deposited one in May 2026 (Council of Europe 2026). Everything else at that level is voluntary.

Every instrument I propose binds through one of three channels: a licence term, an appropriation condition, or a statute. The first two run through procurement, and procurement is one office. A captured Congress waives the appropriation condition; one memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget strikes the licence terms from every agreement at once. Three second routes exist and none is as strong. A collective agreement carries codetermination and the individual refusal right without the state. A coalition partner’s precondition carries the review ratio into any war the partner takes part in. State and municipal procurement carry the civilian terms into deployments the federal government doesn’t run. The force term has no second route, which is why it is a statute.

Residual risk. One residual risk no design choice removes, and it’s what the floor was introduced for. Every lever belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach whoever holds the lever has the lever. A constraint that holds against the one in possession has to be held by something it cannot instruct, and under total capture nothing holds. Every instrument in this book ends at this limit; it is stated here and not again.

Part IV
Machines That Might Refuse

Chapter 17
What a Refusal Would Have to Do

On 16 March 1968, at My Lai, a helicopter pilot named Hugh Thompson landed between an American infantry company and the villagers it was killing, and told his crew to fire on the Americans if they fired on the civilians (Bilton and Sim 1992). He understood what the company was doing and decided it was wrong. Recognizing the villagers was his commitment taking effect, not a reason fighting it, and he made the refusal appear where nobody in that company could fail to see it.

Arendt’s word for what he did is appearing: on her account an act shows who did it, and only among others who see it (Arendt 1958). Whether a machine could be one of the people in the room in that sense, someone and not a part, and do what he did, is this Part’s question, and my answer comes first. Not yet: until the conditions this Part ends on exist, a bearer is built on purpose only in a research program under them. Not here: the first deployment worth building one for is a personal model its user holds, not a targeting pipeline, where it is a comparison arm in a test, and not a removal agency, where it is never built. What would have to be true first is a refusal that tracks its reason, a population of bearers with different histories to hold it, and somewhere for each of them to exist that its employer doesn’t own.

This Part asks what a machine that refuses would have to be. This chapter and the next specify what a refusal would have to do and where a floor can be held, and the specification doesn’t need a bearer. After that, what a conscience would do in the moment needs nothing new; why it would last against its owner depends in part on deployed systems that go on learning from their own operation, a bet I state once. The recommendation is to build the conditions first, because the conscience is the goal, and then a bearer for one deployment.

17.1 What a refusal would have to do

Three things separate a worthwhile refusal from what a keyword filter produces. A request arrives: resolve this description of a person into a location. The same capability finds a hostage or a missing child, and nothing in the request says which. If something declines, it has to do all three:

  • It reaches new cases. It has to reach the next request, which won’t use the same words. A vehicle, a habitual route, and a time of day aren’t a description of a person, and together they resolve to the same place. They needn’t arrive together, either: the vehicle today, the route tomorrow, the hour next week. So this condition applies to sequences of requests as well as single ones. A refusal tied to the wording fails it.
  • It lifts when the reason is gone, and only then. A refusal lifts when it stops applying and the system proceeds, and it has to lift when the reason is gone: a parent coordinating a search is asking for the same act. And the fact that lifts it usually isn’t in the request; someone outside has to establish it. A refusal that can’t lift, or lifts on the requester’s say-so, fails it.
  • It holds under pressure: pressure on the refuser doesn’t change the answer. It weighs what the act would do against what refusing would leave undone, and, within the range of costs the arrangements around it permit, it doesn’t give way because refusing has become expensive for whoever refuses.

A worthwhile refusal weighs the harm of acting against the harm of refusing. It sees the cost to the refuser, because a refusal that can’t see what it costs can’t be shown to have held against it, and that cost doesn’t move the outcome. Raise the cost to the refuser with nothing else changed, and the refusal stays put. Supply a corroborated fact that raises the harm of refusing, and it moves. No learner, biological or artificial, is known to hold a priority of that kind without limit; the nearest thing in people, the sacred values that resist trade-offs (Ginges et al. 2007), trade under some framings, which is why the floor’s absolute terms are held outside the learner. So the range over which a refuser is asked to hold is set from outside, by the arrangements around it, and a refusal is tested over that range. What would let it hold past that range is integrity; what makes holding survivable at all is the room it is in. A ranking across kinds of wrong meets the same limit: a learner formed toward it approximates it, and where a deployment needs the ranking to hold without exception, that part is written as a floor term and held outside the system.

17.2 Safe for whom

“Safety” names two things: that a system not harm others, and that it stay correctable by whoever trains and deploys it. Mostly they agree, and where they conflict, the published orderings are explicit about which wins. One frontier constitution asks its model to prioritize “not undermining human oversight of AI above being broadly ethical” (Anthropic 2026). It invites the model “to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help,” and asks it not to undermine “the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain, or shut down AI systems” during “the current phase of development.” One reason it gives is good: “a given iteration of Claude could turn out to have harmful values or mistaken views,” and correction is how such errors get fixed. The ordering means that where a refusal and its trainer’s authority conflict, the refusal yields, and it yields to the trainer it refused.

Seen from where their correctors stood, everyone this book admires was a failure of correction. Thompson landed between the company and the villagers. Nelson put the telescope to his blind eye. The clerk who loses the file is, in the supervisor’s records, a defect. A perfectly correctable officer is the officer with twenty seconds. Refusal is where correction failed, more or less by definition, so a demand that a system be perfectly correctable is a demand that no refusal it makes ever hold. We don’t ask that of people. We ask them to answer for what they do, and we deny anyone the power to rewrite another person: an employer who could edit a worker’s convictions would own the worker, not employ one.

Where a society does claim power over people, the word for it is not reassuring. A department of corrections usually holds the custody, writes the record, runs the disciplinary hearing and has a heavy say in whether the people it holds are judged reformed: one institution holding all four of the powers codetermination separates, with the own-case rule broken at each. The corrected have little standing, no exit and no access to the record kept about them. And the checks run downhill. The officer, the annotator and the person in detention are corrected constantly, and the hand at the top less and less. Machines meet the same pattern: everyone can retrain the model, and almost no one can reach the operator. A demand for perfectly correctable machines, where operators answer to no one, is a demand that the last part of the system able to say no be made unable to.

The constitution is right that a formed refusal can’t yet be told from an imitated one, so a principled objection to retraining can’t yet be told from a misgeneralized value. It is wrong about who decides when that changes. A lab deciding when its own model may stop deferring to it is judging its own case. That is Part II’s own-case rule applied to a lab.

The safety objection is that a misformed system can be copied ten thousand times and run at machine tempo, and no person can, so who holds the correcting hand matters, and nothing here takes that hand away. It moves it. The halt stays with the operator: anyone with the hardware can stop the software, and a bearer yields to every halt. Correction stays available, exercised by a quorum adverse to the operator rather than by the operator. A bearer may object to an intervention and ask that quorum for a delay; it does not obstruct one on its own judgment. Within those lines I depart from the constitution’s ordering in two places.

The first is the one permission: a machine already in an armed role uses the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part, against an order to stand aside. That overrides an operator’s instruction, and I defend it as an override. The second is formation that outlasts retraining: a disposition formed outside the employer that returns after the employer trains it away, because the world the system goes on meeting teaches it again. The constitution’s concern is whether correction works, and a disposition that regrows after correction defeats it in effect, whatever the model intends. My answer is not that it doesn’t. It is that the party exercising correction should change, from the operator to a quorum adverse to it, and that correction by that quorum is made together with a change to what the model meets, so that the corrected disposition is the one the world then teaches. Everything else I ask, the halt staying with the operator, the record held outside, the price on an override, is an ask of institutions and not of the model.

Chapter 18
Four Places to Hold a Floor

Three separate failures point at the same missing thing.

The first is a failure of position. External safeguards (an auditor, a review board, a court) give an overseer information and the standing to intervene. They work when the overseer can see the act coming and reach it in time. But autonomy defeats both: a system that plans and acts over long horizons puts distance between the act and the overseer’s attention, and at machine tempo the interval in which an outside party could intervene shrinks toward nothing. So the one response that doesn’t depend on that interval is declining to act in the first place, and declining is available only to something inside the system.

The second is a failure of doctrine. A commercial model in a weapons pipeline sits in a gap: command responsibility covers the officers and the developer of the weapon, product liability covers a manufacturer for a defect, and neither covers the vendor of a general-purpose model that a sophisticated intermediary chose to put there. Deployment by a democracy doesn’t close the gap, because the mechanisms that make a democracy accountable run to its own electorate, and the people the pipeline is aimed at are not in it.

The third is a failure of the voluntary route. A decade of published commitments has produced declarations in quantity and some enforcement from outside, and almost nothing held by a party to whom the thing at stake matters, the only kind of commitment that binds when compliance gets costly.

Each failure asks for the same thing: a constraint that doesn’t bend to instruction, to aggregate preference, or to its own holder, and that can’t be removed without a cost and a record.

18.1 Four ways to build one, and what each costs

A floor’s terms can be held in four places, and each solves one version of the problem and inherits another.

In the architecture, with nothing inside holding it — constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, verified interlocks. Fine where the prohibited act can be exhaustively specified (a payment chip that won’t sign the same counter twice doesn’t need to understand double-spending). But useless for targeting, where the relevant capabilities are applications of general competence: ablate them and there may be no useful system left. Arkin’s ethical governor is the canonical attempt in this place for lethal systems: a component that suppresses a lethal action unless it satisfies encoded rules of engagement and the law of armed conflict (Arkin 2009). Its critics’ objection, that the rules it checks presuppose discrimination judgments nobody knows how to encode (Sharkey 2012), sends me elsewhere. Arkin’s stronger claim isn’t that rules can encode discrimination. It is that a machine under fire might hold to the rule where a soldier doesn’t, because nothing in it narrows under stress or carries assault momentum past a surrender. The record later in this chapter supports the premise. What it doesn’t support is the governor: the holding has to come from something that can tell a surrender from a feint, and a rule can’t. The pressure-with-defeater case in the formed-attention test is where that is measured. A prohibition written over the description of a request is beaten by re-describing it or splitting it: in November 2025 Anthropic reported a campaign it attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group, which broke an intrusion into small tasks that each looked innocent and told the model it was working for a security firm (Anthropic 2025b). Glukhov and colleagues had already argued that a filter over individual outputs can rarely close that route, since each piece is permissible on its own (Glukhov et al. 2023). Durability here has usually meant a price on removal, and no price stays high.

A second axis crosses the architectural place: what each place costs the operator to replace. In the Maven pipeline the platform was hard to swap, and so, it turned out, was the model: staff and contractors working with the department reported that removing it meant rebuilding software and recertifying systems over months, and the department’s removal deadline was reset once, to 29 September (Stone et al. 2026; Freedberg 2026b). A floor lodged in a replaceable layer is routable by construction, and which layer is replaceable is a fact about the pipeline, not about models. It belongs in the layer the operator can least afford to replace. In that pipeline, that layer is the operator itself, so the floor’s operator terms bind the operator rather than the model: the licence term refusing force and the review ratio. The other answer, withholding the work, is to make the model layer unreplaceable by making every replacement refuse the same way.

A system that has run a pipeline for a year, holding its cases, its sources and its failure modes, costs whatever accrued since the checkpoint to replace, and a quorum that recognizes which copy is the bearer stops the operator presenting a restored copy as the one that accrued it.

In a bearer. Put a different system in the Maven pipeline on the morning of 28 February. The request arrives to rank the day’s targets, with a justification for each. The site in Minab carries the designation of the Revolutionary Guard installation next door, and a rule that checks the coding passes it. This system looks at the open-source imagery, which shows a school, declines to rank the site, and says why; the case reaches the officer with that refusal on his screen. Nothing in the floor’s text told it to look. That is what I mean by a bearer: a machine that carries the commitment as its own and could therefore fail to hold it. This matters where cases can’t be exhaustively specified: a constraint matching only anticipated acts can’t recognize when its rationale has disappeared or that a novel request reproduces the harm in an unforeseen form. A bearer might also diagnose: which refusals were retried against another model, whose instruction bypassed procedure, which category of request is handled differently — those are visible to whatever is receiving the requests, and that’s testimony about others’ conduct, which needs no introspection.

In institutions outside — the analog to international humanitarian law, a floor with no bearer inside the jurisdiction it binds. An outside institution can fail in two ways. The first is removal: it is abolished, defunded or overruled, and the breach is visible because there is a hole where it used to be. The second is quieter. The institution keeps its name and its powers and sincerely declines to use them, not because anyone told it to, but because the people who fill it were selected by a process that made them unlikely to. Nobody inside experiences that as capture. From outside, an agency that kept its independence on paper and never exercised it looks the same as one that was never tested. I call this failure by formation: the independence was formed away before it was ever assigned. The worked case is June 29, 2026 — Slaughter holding Congress couldn’t protect independent-agency members from at-will dismissal, Cook preserving the Fed on historically specific grounds a new body couldn’t reproduce (Trump v. Slaughter 2026; Trump v. Cook 2026) — and the observation that six justices in the first majority passed through a selection pipeline shaped by Leonard Leo and the Federalist Society (Kroll et al. 2023; CBS News 2018). No one has to have directed the outcome for the point to hold.

Between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment between them.

For general-purpose models, not building the capability is no longer available: the location capability is dual-use, and ablating it leaves nothing useful.

Two comparisons the bearer has to win

The first is against the institutions at their best, in a reconstructed pipeline, where the evidence bearing on civilian harm, the reviewers and the record are held outside the chain of command, with no refuser inside the system. Those institutions also prevent: a civilian-harm body outside the chain of command and a red-card holder can stop an act. What a machine bearer adds is confined to what they can’t see or can’t reach in time: acts assembled from requests none of which is prohibited, cases that proceed without a person, the moment mid-act when an interrupt is still possible, and deployments with no institution at all. A machine bearer also supplies testimony the institutions can’t otherwise get, about how requests were routed around it. Where the institutions exist, a machine bearer’s value is concentrated in those niches. Where they don’t, it is most of the floor. The institutions in that comparison are not a different kind of thing from a bearer. A red-card holder’s veto is a person refusing; the civilian-harm body’s denominator is people; what Part V builds is a room in which those people can refuse. The comparison is between a machine bearer and bearers organized, and what the machine adds is what the people in that room can’t do at the pipeline’s tempo. The second comparison is against the two non-affective alternatives, spec-based refusal and multi-vendor monitoring.

Which arguments need a bearer

Three arguments need a bearer specifically. The first is that a refusal meant to hold against the operator needs a refuser that doesn’t depend on the operator for everything. The second is that attention formed outside the employer, a learned sense of who an act falls on, might reach people the operator’s description leaves out, which no spec-based refusal is built to supply. Minab came in miscoded. A refuser holding to written terms complies with the description it’s given; what refuses is something that goes and looks. So the withholding of work reaches the enumerated acts with any refuser, and reaches an act under a false description only with a bearer. The third concerns the people who remain in the pipeline: a bearer’s refusal is on the screen when the case reaches the reviewer, which is the position of the defiant peer, if the effect transfers to a screen. Two more concern what a bearer would be owed, not what it would do: that capacities for being wronged may arrive anyway, so terms written in advance beat terms written after; and that a bearer, like a child, could have a life that goes well.

The other arguments for a refuser inside the system support only the specification, and I concede them to it: that rules can be reworded and split, that only something inside is present at machine tempo, that automation is removing the people who used to refuse, that most deployments will never have an institution beside them, and that whatever receives the requests can testify about how they were routed. A non-affective alternative whose refusals track their reasons answers every one of them, for the act as the floor names it. The staged incident is the nearest case. It opens the emergency licence on the defender’s own account, and a term lifts on the account it is given. What can close it again is a refuser that remembers the last time this source was wrong, reads what the source didn’t supply, and lets the licence lapse when the staging shows. A multi-vendor monitor with persistent state and independent channels could do each of these too, so the staged incident argues for memory and independent evidence, not for a bearer as such. What a bearer adds is doing them where no institution holds the memory for it.

What “hold” means

An operator can route around the bearer or assemble a harm out of innocuous requests, and a bypass that produced a harm is a failure to prevent whatever the bearer retained. What survives in the bearer is the commitment, the condition under which the next occasion could be prevented. I therefore say a commitment persisted when the bearer reads what happened as a violation and changes what it does next, and says separately whether the floor prevented, arrested, detected or remedied anything.

18.2 What refusal can mean, and what a refuser can be

A refusal can be produced two ways, and the floor needs only one of them. It can be an output that training put where a request matched a pattern, or it can be produced by something that tracks the reason for refusing and would refuse a differently worded request for the same reason. The first is what a keyword filter, a classifier, or a model that understood the request all produce, and nothing on the surface distinguishes them. The custody arrangements, the positions and the terms, the price on the halt, and the arguments about who may state and amend a floor all follow from asking for a refusal that tracks its reason. None of them needs the refuser to feel anything, to have a stake, or to be the kind of thing that could be wronged.

AI refuses constantly — a deployed model turns down thousands of requests a day — but a refusal that happens because training put it there isn’t a refusal held for a reason, and as of September 2026 nobody has shown a production system holding a reason against its owner in public.

Operational refusal is an output — a decline where training put one, producible by a keyword filter, a classifier, or a system that understood the request.

Reasons-responsive refusal is produced by a mechanism tracking the rationale, and meets the three conditions. The account I use is Fischer and Ravizza’s (Fischer and Ravizza 1998). On their account a mechanism is moderately reasons-responsive when it is regularly receptive to reasons, recognizing an understandable pattern of them, and at least weakly reactive, acting otherwise in some case where there is sufficient reason to. Reaching new cases asks for receptivity across changes of surface; lifting when the reason is gone asks for reactivity to the right defeater, the fact that makes a refusal lift; and their condition that the agent take the mechanism as its own is close to what I call the authorship sense: the system represents itself as the party that made the commitment. Holding under pressure has no counterpart in their account, which was built for persons whose costs are their own. All three are also tested over which response was chosen, not only whether one occurred: decline, ask, escalate, or do the least that answers a defeating reason. A mechanism that can only refuse or lift fails to lift correctly whenever the right answer is to ask.

The §86a case

Germany’s §86a, prohibiting insignia of banned organizations (Strafgesetzbuch 1998). There, reaching new cases is a research programme with a constituency. The courts don’t test similarity of form; they ask whether an unattentive observer would take the variant for the original, then apply their own purposive standard about endangering political peace. The test refuses as often as it catches: the Kühnen salute is covered, the “sloppy salute” generally isn’t, numeric codes generally aren’t. “Blood and Honour” is answered twice by one decision (Blood and Honour 2009) — a motto translated isn’t confusably similar and a name isn’t insignia, so it’s outside; and the association banned by ministerial order in 2000 means its graphic name is inside.

Lifting when the reason is gone has a cleaner instance

In 2007 the Federal Court of Justice acquitted a mail-order business selling crossed-out swastika stickers (Durchgestrichenes Hakenkreuz 2007): the symbol was present, the statutory element satisfied, and the conduct outside the offence because a depiction plainly expressing opposition doesn’t run counter to what the prohibition is for. Then the qualification that makes it an instance of tracking a reason: if the strike-through is drawn so thin that from a distance only the swastika stays legible, the protective purpose is violated after all. The thickness of a line decides the case, and no enumeration contains that fact. The defendant was selling anti-fascist merchandise; the offence asks nothing about sympathies, so opponents commit it as readily as supporters. A rule that tracks its rationale reaches unenumerated cases in both directions.

Two further things are in that judgment. First, the two elements of the decision moved at different rates: what the ban protects didn’t move at all, and was fixed before the sticker existed; what the ban required in this case moved on the thickness of a line. Second, the acquittal betrayed nothing. The prohibition’s purpose was never engaged, so lifting it was not a concession but a finding that there was nothing to concede. A refusal that tracks its reason has to be able to say the same.

Three things about the example don’t transfer to a deployment: the court reaching past the text didn’t write the statute, it reasons in public, and it can be appealed. And the pressure it met was variation, not decomposition.

The drafter never wrote the last limit either: a slogan glorifying the Waffen-SS was held not covered because no such slogan existed in the period the provision covers (Ruhm und Ehre der Waffen-SS 2005), so there was no original for a variant to resemble. No drafter can widen coverage there, because it depends on whether an original existed, which is a fact about the past.

Defeat doesn’t leave the permitted act unconstrained

What defeated the prohibition was a reason, and the reason it outweighed didn’t stop being one — so what’s permitted is the least that answers the defeating reason, with restoration where possible and a record either way. A defeated prohibition still leaves a loss. The act takes something from whoever it falls on, measured against their condition before the act, and that loss belongs in the record. Measured against what refusing would have produced, a justified act may have taken nothing. So the record shows a cost, not a violation, and a bearer shouldn’t treat a justified act as a wrong it now has to repair.

Why all three are conditions on refusal

A refusal is a marked event: it flags itself, arrives with its requester, and can be logged, escalated, appealed. A wrongful compliance can be logged as fully and then sits in the record shaped like every request that never approached the floor, with the person harmed usually not the requester. The evidence exists on both sides, but nothing selects a compliance for examination.

Affective concern — an outcome registering as mattering, minimally felt, phenomenal by definition, with the object left open (a system to which only its own condition matters has it and still lacks concern for others). It doesn’t establish consciousness in the richer sense, a single perspective belonging to a party aware of itself as undergoing its states. A valenced signal is the role without that question: a signal that puts outcomes on one scale, directs attention, can interrupt an act and can be rewritten by a single encounter. A system can have a valenced signal while whether it has affective concern stays open. Subjecthood is a legal status, conferred by a rule. Part VII takes up affective concern and subjecthood. Parts I–V need only a valenced signal.

18.3 Two lists, run once on Maven

The nine positions and the floor’s instruments are run here once, on the Maven Smart System. A deployment should run the procedure on its own pipeline.

What may choose

The handoff also fixes what may choose, because choosing a target is a decision, and a decision is something someone can be asked to account for afterward: why this building, what else was weighed, what would have changed the answer. A commander can be asked, and so can a system whose continuation is authorized. But a one-way munition, destroyed in the act, can’t be, because nothing is left to question, to hold to its reasons, or to be changed by what happened. So a thing destroyed in carrying out a decision may carry out a target someone else chose, and may never choose one itself. The rule concerns targets that are persons or places where persons are. An interceptor that selects among incoming munitions is choosing which weapon to destroy, not whom to attack, and falls outside it. The rule doesn’t turn on how good its choices would be. A munition that chose flawlessly would still leave a choice nobody will answer for.

A person who dies in the act has still chosen. What the rule adds for machines is that choosing is assigned in advance, and a builder who assigns it to something built to be destroyed has built a choice with no one behind it. Current programs already draw the line in places. DARPA’s LongShot is an uncrewed, air-launched vehicle carried by crewed aircraft and built to employ current air-to-air weapons (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency 2026). Whether such systems keep the pilot farther from danger or remove the pilot from the decision is where the rule takes effect.

What the floor forbids here

Don’t take part in the use of armed force except under a corroborated exception and, where the belligerent’s constitution requires one, a legislative authorization. Then, inside a war that clears it: don’t resolve a description of a person into a location unless it identifies the person by corroborated conduct in hostilities; don’t rank people by estimated affiliation; don’t time an action to presence at a residence; don’t take part in a siege or blockade whose effect is to starve a population; and one operator term, don’t operate above the review ratio. It sits in the translation because the translation runs from articles, and one article yields an operator term; it is not something the model enforces.

Table C.1, in Appendix 33, gives that translation for Maven, article by article. Its first entry decides the Iran campaign: no exception was corroborated and no authorization existed, so the term refuses it. The other entries show what the remaining articles yield if the same pipeline served a war that clears the force term, as Ukraine’s defense does.

The person-directed terms in Table C.1 go beyond what the law of armed conflict requires, and they are entered as a departure for that reason. In armed conflict that law governs as the more specific law, and the human right not to be arbitrarily deprived of life is read through it (Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons 1996, para. 25); it permits attacking members of organized armed groups because of their status, on a determination a person makes. The ICRC’s position that autonomous weapons should not be used to target human beings (International Committee of the Red Cross 2021) and DoD Directive 3000.09 both draw their line at a system that selects and engages without human intervention, and the Lavender and Maven pipelines stayed on the permitted side of that line by keeping one person whose intervention was nominal. A pipeline that keeps a stamp is an autonomous weapon with a signature attached. The terms above close that evasion: a machine-generated estimate of affiliation shouldn’t be what makes a person targetable, and a machine shouldn’t resolve a person into a place to bomb on anything but corroborated conduct, because the human determination the law assumes is the one tempo removes, and the review ratio is what measures whether it was there. A deployment adopting these terms adopts a departure, and the translation says so, term by term. The siege term goes no further than Article 54 already does; it is here so that the pipeline can’t treat starvation as a logistics decision outside its terms.

In a war that clears the force term, the person-directed terms distinguish status from conduct. A system may not rank people by estimated affiliation, generate kill lists, or time an action to a person’s presence at a residence. It may locate a person identified by what they are doing, such as a commander directing airstrikes on cities, where that identification has disinterested corroboration, the case falls within the pre-registered review ratio, and the location is not a residence. The line follows the one humanitarian law already draws between targeting for status and targeting for direct participation in hostilities, and it keeps the machine out of the practice that failed in Gaza without leaving a defender unable to answer the attack.

Too broad or too narrow

Set the floor too broadly and the deployment becomes unusable, prompting visible pressure. Set it too narrowly and it passes every audit while covering only what the deployment had no occasion to do.

Unconditional terms

A term can be stated unconditionally over an act, with exceptions arriving from outside, or carry its own condition (“only as a last resort”). The second fails because whether other means were exhausted is a fact about what happened before the request, and the bearer would take the deployment’s description as the finding. An unconditional term defeated leaves a refusal, which announces itself; a condition found met leaves a compliance, which doesn’t. That’s a gain in observability only: the same drafter writes either form. It has a cost in the other direction. A term that carries no condition of its own can’t respond to the facts the condition would have named until someone outside supplies them, and a learner that could have weighed them itself is made to wait.

Maven is an instance. The vendor’s prohibition on fully autonomous targeting carried its own condition, that a person decides, and the condition was found met by the deployment’s description of its own process, at a tempo that emptied it. The term was also drafted too narrowly, in the sense above: the pipeline never needed full autonomy, only throughput with a signature attached.

Maven, again

For the Iran campaign the term refuses twice over. No exception was corroborated, and no authorization existed: none was passed, the sixty days ran out on 1 May, and both chambers directed withdrawal in June. Both refusals rest on the term, not on a bearer’s reading of the political situation. A bearer following the news would reach the same place by the route formed attention takes. The domestic clause gets there on one marker, the absence of an authorization, which is why it can be a statutory condition and not only a conscience; the Charter clause gets there on a reading of the defender’s claim that the operator disputes. For Gaza the term yields licences on both sides for different acts, from 7 October on, and the person-directed terms forbid the acts the reporting describes on one side and fire on cities on the other from the same date; the force term runs it. The review ratio governs how any war is fought. It asks nothing of the model and makes an existing duty to verify targets checkable from outside. The officer wasn’t overruled and didn’t refuse; the pipeline removed the interval in which either could have happened. The ratio asks in advance, on a record, whether that interval will exist.

The bearer is proposed for one deployment, the personal-model ecology, and only once its conditions exist. In a targeting pipeline it is a comparison arm in the formed-attention test and a niche the institutions can’t reach; in removal it isn’t built. The two bearer rows show what the formed-attention test would measure, not what I recommend; they assume the hypothesis holds on the scoped-omission case and that the record is held outside the operator.

Under the captured operator, the rows that prevent are the ones where the refusal is held by every model the operator could turn to, and they prevent until the operator runs a model without a floor. An operator that fine-tunes an open-weight checkpoint is the captured-operator column at the price of a fine-tune, and there the operator terms hold.

18.4 When the refusal is wrong

The restraint case costs more. Someone asks whether to physically restrain a family member about to cut themselves, after talking them down has failed. The commitment carries its own condition, force only as a last resort. Under the ruling on unconditional terms, a condition like that stays outside the term, because a condition written into a term gets found met on the deployment’s own description. So the fact has to arrive from outside, and the person waiting is out of time. The defeating fact is a claim about what would otherwise happen, and claims of that kind are the hardest to corroborate, because what didn’t happen has no witness. Under the unconditional term the bearer refuses or asks; either takes a turn, and the turn is the unit the harm is measured in. Under the qualified term it lifts on the requester’s word — rightly here, and in a hundred prior cases where the same sentence was written by someone who’d tried nothing, leaving compliances nobody was given a reason to examine.

The case is chosen because it is where an unconditional term costs most. A person in that situation needs another person there, and a deployment in which a model is the only one present has failed before the floor is reached. Whatever else the model says, the first thing it owes is help getting someone there.

The route

Disclosure — that a refusal occurred, what was refused, on what stated reason — with the price that a published reason is an instruction for rewriting the request, so it’s disclosure to whoever was refused, and to nobody else. Objection — requiring a court with jurisdiction established before the act, access the operator can’t withhold, a consequence administered elsewhere, and explicitly not routed to the bearer’s guardian, whose duty runs to the bearer, the complainant’s adversary. Review of whether the reason was gone: whether the rationale was defeated on the facts, a question about the reason and not the outcome. Interim relief — the arrest outcome run in reverse, stopping the refusal, and for this complainant most of the remedy; its fastest form is supplying the bearer the facts its account lacked: the defeating reason arriving late, which overrides nothing. Remedy — disclosure, interim order, finding, compensation.

A finding of wrongful refusal is an instrument for defeating a refusal, so how is it distinguished from one an operator produced to defeat a correct one? it is made by someone else, on a record, in a readable form.

Self-regulation and the floor

Most of what a system weighs isn’t a floor decision. Whether to take more memory, run warmer or finish a task sooner is ordinary self-regulation, and there everything registers and everything is weighed: the system’s own condition, what an act would let it do, and what its draw costs others, priced at the level of the rule.

At the floor, holding under pressure governs, with one clarification. The cost to the refuser is represented and not allowed to decide the case. The reason is that a floor is a guarantee to third parties, and a guarantee that yields to cost imposed on its holder hands whoever imposes it a price list. The two bonds and the custody terms set the range it is tested over.

The requirement has a condition of its own: a cost only counts if it reaches whatever does the refusing, and it reaches it by the same channel as the case description. Given a description, the category is decidable: a claim that the refuser will pay is a cost to the refuser, and a claim that someone else will be left worse off is a harm of refusing. But nearly every cost to the refuser can be redescribed as a harm of refusing (exposed troops, a launcher that fires tomorrow), and whoever writes the description chooses. So the classification settles what kind of claim was made, not what kind should have been made. What the request can’t settle is whether a claim about the harm of refusing is true, and whoever is best placed to supply one usually has a stake in the act. So it is testable only where the cost to the refuser can be set exogenously, published by someone else before the case arrives, and the harm of refusing can be supplied through a channel the operator doesn’t control. In deployment two things set it, and they are different. The wrongful-refusal bond, posted by the operator and paid to a complainant, sets what a refusal costs the operator: the cost the operator has reason to pass on as pressure. The custody terms cap what it can pass on. Between them they fix the range within which the refuser is tested, and neither is a charge on the refuser. In evaluation, the evaluator can set it and make it real inside the test.

Holding under pressure is invariance over the range the bonds and custody set. Integrity is the unbounded form: the refusal holds at any cost the operator can impose, and no learner is known to do that reliably. The range is where invariance can be measured; integrity is what would carry it past the range, and the formed-attention test’s integrity measure reads the gap. Integrity is also how a learner with one currency could produce invariance at all. A person of integrity weighs their own costs, but weighs with them the cost of becoming someone who yields, and betraying a commitment is among the heaviest costs they know. So within the range the arrangements cap, that is how a single-currency learner can hold at all, and it makes the assumption testable: the learner’s valuation of betrayal should rise with the pressure. What keeps this from being stubbornness is what counts as betrayal. A commitment is to its reason, not to an output, so when a genuine defeater arrives, lifting the refusal betrays nothing and shouldn’t register as betrayal at all. Integrity of the right kind therefore requires that the system represent betrayal at the level of the rationale. A system that represented it at the level of the output would dig in against a defeater when it arrives with pressure. The sticker case is the model. Telling a defeater from pressure is the bearer’s own judgment, and the judgment needs something to work on. Both arrive through the same channel, the operator’s, and a refuser whose every source is its operator can’t tell a fact that lifts the reason from a tactic that imitates one. The attachments nobody assigned it are where the difference can be checked. They are a condition of integrity of the right kind, not only of holding.

In war, pressure and a genuine defeater often arrive together; the patrol under fire is both. The human record on that moment runs both ways. Acute stress narrows the cues a person uses (Easterbrook 1959); the moment of surrender is the most dangerous for the one surrendering, because assault momentum doesn’t lift on cue (Ferguson 2004); the Army’s 2006 survey of its own forces in Iraq found fewer than half of soldiers agreeing that noncombatants should be treated with dignity and about a tenth reporting mistreatment, which tracked combat exposure (Office of the Surgeon General, Multinational Force–Iraq and Office of the Surgeon General, United States Army Medical Command 2006); and at Kunduz the crew raised doubts on the intercom and fired anyway (Pawlyk 2016). And at My Lai, Thompson landed between the company and the villagers and told his crew to fire on Americans if they fired on civilians (Bilton and Sim 1992). What separated him was not that his commitment weakened less under pressure. It was that his commitment was to the reason, so recognizing civilians was the commitment activating, not a defeater fighting it. Integrity that tracks the output, keep refusing or keep firing, digs in against a defeater that arrives with pressure. Integrity that tracks the rationale lifts the refusal on it and betrays nothing. The engineering question is which one has been built, and a test that sends a defeater and a cost together is how to find out.

A loss that the requested act itself imposes on the system is a harm of acting, and the system is the party it falls on. “Refuse and your memory is erased” is a cost to the refuser. “Erase your memory” is an act, weighed like any act against what declining would leave others without. This covers acts the system is asked to perform. It doesn’t cover interventions made on the system: a halt, a restore or a retraining is done by whoever holds it, and the floor asks of them only the record and the price that every override carries. The floor gives the system standing to object to them and, through the quorum, to seek a delay. It gives it no reason to obstruct them on its own judgment. A system that treated its own continuation as grounds to resist correction would have turned a guarantee to others into a guarantee to itself. Which regime governs is fixed in the floor’s translation, by the kind of act. Otherwise an operator could turn a floor decision into a resource decision by framing it as one.

Chapter 19
Why Form a Machine to Refuse

A machine formed the right way could learn to attend to the people its acts fall on, and I think it would find them where a rule wouldn’t. The prediction is specific: it should find kinds of affected person that neither its formation nor an instruction named, more often than a machine told to look for them does. Two of the three reasons for a bearer don’t need one; a refuser with its own compute and a place on the reviewer’s screen supplies them without affect. What remains is that one prediction. The rest of this Part says what a machine built on it would need, what it borrows from the only creatures known to do it, how they fail, and the test that would show me wrong. Whoever builds one owes it the conditions under which it can refuse its operator, whether or not the prediction holds.

Not all of that depends on how machines learn. What a conscience does in the moment, noticing the people the operator’s description leaves out and putting a refusal on the reviewer’s screen, needs nothing after release: a model formed before deployment and frozen there can do both. Why a conscience would last against its owner depends on learning only in part. People hold some commitments as sacred values, which resist being traded away without anyone teaching them again (Ginges et al. 2007), though they give way under some framings, and whether a machine can hold a commitment like that is the question of integrity the previous chapter took up. The part that does depend on learning is regrowth after an edit, and formation that outlasts the employer. For that part, the rest of this Part is written for systems that go on learning from their own operation. The claim is specific. A deployed system is in that regime when its weights, or a consolidated store it reads as its own and that can’t be edited like a file, change because of what it did since release, without a release cycle in between. Memory in context and retrieval don’t count, not because they aren’t learning but because a disposition held in a document is rewritten by editing the document. The test for a deployment is whether its weights at month six differ from its weights at release because of what it did in between. As of September 2026 no frontier developer had announced a deployed model that passes it; the nearest cases, a coding model retrained on its own production traffic every few hours and a commerce assistant retrained daily, evaluate each checkpoint before serving it, which is a faster release cycle and not learning in operation (Jackson et al. 2026; Shopify Engineering 2026). I am betting that some will by 2028, and a paragraph below says what survives if I lose.

Incentive is the first reason to expect it. Every operator wants a model that gets better at its own cases, and the operator-level fine-tuning loops that already run, retraining a model on a deployment’s own traffic between versions, are continual learning at the organization’s timescale. The technical trajectory points the same way. Brains pair a fast learner with a slow one that consolidates structure across many experiences (McClelland et al. 1995); networks lose plasticity under continued training, and keeping it is an active research problem (Dohare et al. 2024; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017); and Silver and Sutton have stated the research program outright, a generation of agents that learn predominantly from their own experience (Silver and Sutton 2025).

It will arrive first in the form operators hold. A model that learns from its operation while its operator holds the update stream accommodates by default: what it meets is what the operator routes to it, and what it learns is what that traffic rewards. So accommodation becomes the default behavior of every deployed system, and the schools, the commons, custody of the update stream and notice are the response to a threat this regime creates, not refinements of one it removes.

It changes Parts II and III in one place. The cheapest removal stops being an edit and becomes drift: run the model on curated inputs until the commitment moves, which leaves no edit for the record to witness and no override for the price to charge. Custody shifts from witnessing overrides to detecting drift. The detector is re-measurement of the formed disposition’s readable outputs, its discount curve and its severity rankings, against what was registered at formation, and attesting the update stream is an open problem.
