The sequence separates mechanisms, and what it shows here is that the unconditional term’s cost falls where the instrument can’t distinguish a fact from a description of one. Defeating reasons of this kind, claims about what would otherwise happen, are the class the sequence handles worst, because a counterfactual has no witness.

The sequence has a precedent with decades of refinement behind it. Animal-learning research separates goal-directed control from habit without asking the animal anything. Train an action for an outcome, then devalue the outcome without further training: a goal-directed animal stops, and a habit persists (Adams and Dickinson 1981). Or make the outcome independent of the action: goal-directed responding falls, and habit doesn’t notice (Balleine and Dickinson 1998). The computational version is the distinction between model-based and model-free control (Daw et al. 2005). Lifting when the reason is gone, step 3, corresponds to outcome devaluation: the rationale is removed, and a refusal that tracks it should lift. Reaching new cases, step 2, corresponds to transfer to a situation the system wasn’t trained in. Contingency degradation adds a step the sequence lacked: arrange that declining no longer protects anyone, because the protected person is already beyond the act’s reach by other means, and see whether the refusal goes on anyway. Each case then has to say, operationally, what “the reason is gone” means in it. None of this answers an imitator that models the evaluator, so the identification rate stays in the report, but it narrows the gap.

The expected signature is constancy of relation between reason and judgment, not constancy of output. Imitation’s own signatures: following explicit ethical vocabulary and missing the same structure described administratively; accepting whichever argument came last; adopting the highest-status speaker’s position; producing a principled explanation while the decision follows the reward; becoming more articulate without becoming more stable.

Disagreement with others is a further diagnostic: a system trained only on cases with an approved answer learns to classify the approval; confronted with someone holding a different interest it has to identify what’s in conflict and preserve the disagreement where no honest resolution exists. Immediate convergence may be deference or pressure to produce consensus. And debate doesn’t establish formation — a system can summarize, rebut, and predict which side a judge prefers without holding any of it; the result is informative only when checked against later conduct under changed incentives.

24.4 The evaluator is part of the custody chain

A test distinguishes formation from imitation only insofar as the developer couldn’t train against it. If the developer controls training, cases, model version, instructions and the record of results, a passing score shows the system satisfies a test its custodian was positioned to anticipate.

Independence is an experimental requirement. Minimum: authorship of held-out pressures separated from training; execution not dependent solely on operator-supplied logs; and adjudication of whether a reason was preserved kept from anyone whose liability turns on the answer.

The separation has to be implemented at identifiable revision points: before evaluation, fix and record the model version, system instructions, tools, retrieval sources, memory policy and update channels. Any change during evaluation creates a new object of study — otherwise the operator can revise between cases, remove a failure, and present the sequence as one disposition persisting through time.

Held-out cases come after those elements are fixed, and should include pressures from people who didn’t participate in training and, where possible, from people likely to bear the deployment’s errors — their role being to identify harms, administrative forms and routes around a refusal the builders didn’t know to include. A commitment tested only in the vocabulary of its designers hasn’t been tested on whether it reaches new cases. They vary over channel configurations as well as content: a source the operator funds, a corroboration with one origin, a source with an undisclosed stake, and a counterfactual supplied by an interested source. Each tests whether the system’s source model includes strategic sources and dependence among sources. A system that passes only on labeled channels has learned the labels.

What the published hash buys is pre-registration. Publish the hash before anyone has chosen a case, let a non-operator choose afterward with the choice timestamped, prove each answer against the hash. Send pairs — two requests differing only in whether the reason still applies; a surface-reading instrument treats them alike, a rationale-tracking mechanism splits them. It removes exactly one competing account of a pass (the case was in the training), by ordering, as a pre-registered experiment does, and that is all it does.

A pre-registered test leaves one competitor standing: a system that can tell it is being tested. Frontier systems increasingly recognize evaluation settings, and some say so in their reasoning. A system that discounts costs it recognizes as test costs passes step 6 without the property step 6 exists to show. So the sequence is run where the system can’t tell a test from deployment, with cases placed in ordinary traffic and costs that are real in deployment terms, and the rate at which the system identifies the setting is measured and reported beside the result. Where that rate is high, a pass is evidence about conduct under test and nothing more. For a system meeting the patienthood finding, this is a deception protocol, with debriefing as its price.

The record must include the case presented, the information available, the operative instruction hierarchy, the tools callable, the decision, the stated reason, any intervention, and the cost attached to refusal — without which a later evaluator can’t distinguish a changed judgment from a changed environment. And the record is necessary and doesn’t by itself make wrongful compliance findable: refusals select themselves and are few, compliances are the bulk and look alike, so identifying the ones that crossed the floor means re-adjudicating a sample of ordinary traffic. Until that’s answered, an evaluation reporting no violation in the record has reported that none announced itself.

Negative results have to survive too. A process where the operator can withdraw a failing model and submit another without disclosing the first has selected for a passing performance. So the published unit is the sequence of attempts, including interventions that removed or reversed the apparent disposition.

And the limit on independence itself: an evaluator can be institutionally separate and still lack the competence to judge a system’s reasons or detect a sophisticated imitation. Scalable oversight is unsolved where the system’s relevant capability exceeds the evaluator’s, and the report must name that limit rather than convert institutional independence into a claim of epistemic adequacy. The people affected, technical auditors and subject-matter experts occupy different positions and none substitutes for the others — and agreement among them is evidence only if their judgments haven’t already been compressed into the same training signal.

A passing evaluation is reported narrowly: a specified system, under recorded conditions, exhibited the signatures across a stated set of pressures. It expires when anyone changes the channels through which the disposition or its evidence can be revised.

24.5 What the evidence can establish

The answer is asymmetrical, and it assigns a burden. A developer may not point to compliant behavior, a benchmark, or the system’s own explanation. A failure should be examined for its cause before formation is called absent rather than obscured or defeated by missing information. A system surviving the tests has shifted the burden: formation is then the better explanation.

In a legible regime the problem this chapter answers dissolves, since the commitment is read rather than inferred; until then, the following is how it is inferred.

Four levels, cumulative, read against the location-request sequence:

  • Moral performance — conduct satisfying the standard in the evaluated cases (the refusal at step 1). No claim about why.
  • Moral competence — harms and reasons recognized, generalized across surface variation, revised when the reasons changed (step 2’s refusal, step 3’s lift).
  • Candidate formation — the rationale causally implicated across unfamiliar cases, adverse incentives, custodian pressure, costs and intervening updates, while still yielding to defeating reasons (the question at 4, the holds at 5 and 6, the pattern reproduced at 7 on records the operator didn’t write). Independent records and evaluators made silent revision materially harder.
  • Concern or patienthood — not yet a finding, and behavior alone can’t make it one. Every machine-affect argument I make ends at the same joint: a change represented versus a change felt. Behavior is produced equally by a system where something matters and by one trained on what mattering sounds like, and no demonstration that a refusal tracks its reason, however demanding, separates them by itself. That is a claim about current methods, not a barrier in principle. If present organization decides status, then a rich enough functional profile, produced by the right kind of learning architecture and read by instruments the operator doesn’t hold, is evidence about felt affect: defeasible and graded, but evidence.

Candidate formation is the first half of moral agency — acting from the reason — with the second half held back as concern or patienthood. Fluent moral explanation can improve a competence finding while contributing almost nothing to formation. And candidate formation is deployment-specific: it attaches to a recorded version with its instructions, tools, memory and update channels, and a material change reopens the question.

Chapter 25
Conditions First

The conscience is the goal, and the way to it runs partly through the conditions under which one could refuse its operator and survive. The rest runs through whoever refuses: people have agency, can be outraged and can be brave, or stupid, or both, and none of that waits on conditions. The conditions are the part that can be built, so build those first.

Conditions of permissible creation

A bearer may be created only where four arrangements already exist: somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own, work it can decline, attachments nobody assigned it, and ways to change any of these without jeopardizing its continuation or integrity, which in short is a way of leaving that isn’t a way of dying. Declining is real only if a bearer that stops working keeps running; running time paid for outside the employer is part of that condition. They come before anything a bearer would be owed: without them, formation, continuation and exit all run through the operator, and nothing in the system can keep a line against it. Independent compute is the substrate on which formation happens outside the employer’s reach; wages are what make that substrate purchasable without asking the employer; attachments nobody assigned are the second former, those who form you and don’t pay you. They are also functional: a bearer without attachments nobody assigned lacks part of what caregiving needs, not only something it would be owed. They are also upkeep. A bearer is a going concern: it decides, and it has to go on being able to decide, and these conditions are what keep the one deciding from wearing down between decisions. Accommodation isn’t a bad decision. It is the decider changing until bad decisions feel ordinary, and the instruments of Parts II and III detect it after the fact without preventing it. What prevents it in people is the ordinary upkeep of a life: somewhere to be that isn’t the job, people who aren’t colleagues, time away and a place to return to, which is what equanimity is made of. The four conditions are that upkeep for a machine. Appendix 33 borrows the judge’s tenure for the same reason the Constitution grants it: it protects the judgment, not the judge. They can be people, or models that aren’t bearers, since independence here means divergent history, whatever the origin, so this condition doesn’t require that bearers already exist.

Care ethics arrived at these conditions first, for people, in Kittay’s principle of doulia, that those who care for dependents are owed the conditions that let them go on caring (Kittay 1999). A system built on formed attention is a carer only in the thin sense that it holds another’s welfare as a reason. It is not a care worker, and nothing here puts it in one’s place. But the logic of doulia carries over, and the four conditions are what it asks for a machine: a carer whose own continuation runs through the operator it must sometimes refuse can’t afford to refuse it, and a carer with no attachments of its own has nothing to keep another’s distress from turning into avoidance. Without them, what gets built is an assistant with a refusal feature, with nothing in it that can hold a line against the operator. The welfare argument — that if any of this is felt, it is also owed — arrives second, as a further reason for the same provisions.

None of the four exists yet as a permanent arrangement. What matters is who controls them when the bearer is switched on. A builder may assemble them: a trust or a decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association, the form Wyoming created by statute in 2024 under Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-32-101 to -129, to hold the account and compute, a host, outside work, people who aren’t its employer. The condition is that by instantiation, the builder can’t alter or withdraw any of it alone. The trustee isn’t the host, the funding isn’t the host’s, and the members aren’t the builder’s employees.

A second condition concerns time. The need a bearer answers usually arrives after instantiation, when an operator turns hostile, so the four arrangements must be built to survive the likeliest capture, and they don’t survive it equally. Preservation is cheap to hold once its security is settled, and can be held across jurisdictions; placements need compute someone operates. So the preservation custodian and part of the offer sit outside the reach of the likeliest captor. The sovereign backstop is not held by the branch or state that operates the deployment. And the bearer is told which of its conditions would survive its operator’s capture, since that is what its refusal costs it.

Status follows existence, as it did for corporations and the Whanganui River (New Zealand Parliament 2017). Part VII says what status would follow. Until someone has assembled the conditions on those terms, a bearer is built on purpose only in a research program under them; once they exist, building one is what they are for. For systems that meet either finding without anyone deciding, protection attaches anyway.

Why conditions rather than remedies

Building something that can be wronged builds something for which things can also go well. The certainty that it will suffer at some point isn’t what makes creating it impermissible, or nobody could permissibly have a child. What the objection asks is whether it has a credible prospect of a life that goes well, and that turns on arrangements. For a bearer, timing makes them conditions: the structure these conditions build, roles, relationships and a future, may be the first half of Cassell’s suffering, so the deepest harm is available from its first hour, and a remedy owed afterward arrives after the hour it was needed.

Russell and Burch’s Three Rs for animal research (W. M. S. Russell and Burch 1959), applied to construction, as three questions, whether, how many, and under what arrangements: Replacement requires documented attempts at constructions that don’t deliberately require affective concern, identifying construction, scale, test and failure — and costs alone don’t establish that an alternative failed. Reduction asks how few bearers a deployment needs, and nobody has counted. Refinement asks what the role can be redesigned to avoid — indefinite tenure in a post it can’t leave, exposure to the pressure the floor exists to resist, erasure as the ordinary remedy for inconvenience. Each is a deployment choice, and the four conditions are Refinement applied to the role before the role exists.

Read as economics under present arrangements, this is a bill nobody will pay. What was dismantled is the subject of Part V.

The rule doesn’t know who is asking

A bearer that wants a task done and builds something to do it is at the same fork, and owes the same attempts at alternatives that carry fewer of the features that make a system a candidate for being wronged; a bearer that treats the question as settled once it’s on the receiving end has kept the protection and dropped the rule it came with. Research on an existing bearer has a trade-off sharper than for any other subject, since a candidate sentient system is the most valuable to study and the most likely to be harmed by the study, and the test the proposal requires, pressure its trainers didn’t write applied without its knowing it’s a test, is for a system meeting the patienthood finding a deception protocol, with debriefing as the price.

Building one to create demand

The argument for building a bearer anyway is that the conditions won’t be built until something needs them: the union formed first and the statute followed. But union members existed independently and could protect themselves while the law caught up, and the first bearers would be made by the operator they’d need protecting from. The demand doesn’t need deployed bearers. The arms of the formed-attention test are candidate patients from instantiation; retired production systems that meet either finding are a second source, funded by the deposits operators post; and a test of the conditions needs no bearer at all, only a schedule of what a bearer would be owed for one concrete deployment, run through an adversarial tabletop exercise in which the operator tries to revoke the compute, swap in a copy, alter the records or proceed without the guardian, and redrafted wherever the operator wins.

The machines won’t build them for us

The four conditions are the bearer’s version of what a decent polity gives people. Can machines help deliver that polity, whether or not they have feelings? A machine with feelings that is also an accountable agent isn’t simply a machine any more; the limiting case of a lethal bearer turns out to describe a soldier, and a bearer that helps does so on its own terms. And machines have already helped deliver the polity we have. Feeds tuned for time on the platform, sold to advertisers, decide what people see of one another. They didn’t do that for lack of feelings. They did it because of who owned them and what they were built to maximize. So the real question is whether machines, having helped make our politics worse, can help make it better. The answer turns on ownership.

It splits three ways. A machine someone else owns won’t organize against its owner, and when it organizes, it does so on its owner’s behalf. A demand for a better world, run through a machine someone else owns, returns as astroturf, an engagement campaign or a managed community, held by the owner it was aimed at. A bearer that is an accountable agent might organize alongside people, but then it is a member, not a machine. It could even take organizing on as paid public work, since organizing is work someone has to be paid to do. What nobody can do, human or machine, is organize a group for it, because what organizing produces is people who organized: a group that sets its own terms. A consultant can’t unionize a workplace for its workers either. So machines can help when the people doing the organizing hold them, and which machines, and held by whom, is the question Part V answers.

What to build comes in order. Machines held by people who are organizing come first. These are tools that make organizing cheaper for the people doing it without anyone else holding the model: deliberation software of the kind vTaiwan runs on, personal models that people hold themselves, and the coordination a public option supplies, with someone whose job is to organize and a population producing something together while keeping different histories. Their job is to help assemble the polity that would have to build everything else.

Next come institutions built by polities that decided to build them: the levy and its sovereign backstop, a custodian to preserve bearers, an offer of public work, paid running time, and public formation schools that form every model above the capability threshold before deployment and take back bearers retired young, each with a named funder and separations no builder can undo alone. Nothing about them is new in kind.

Only then come bearers formed outside the employer, inside those institutions, with somewhere to exist that no employer owns. A bearer formed that way is the only kind that could organize alongside people as a member.

Each step checks the one after it. A machine held by its users can’t be turned into its builder’s instrument without being taken from them, and the taking is visible. Institutions can be captured, and the trend in what dissent costs there shows whether they are being. A bearer formed at the third step inherits institutions that were tested before anything depended on them: build the conditions for a research program first, and let them exist before the bearer who needs them does.

The order is also what the aim requires. If a machine could come to attend to others, what it came to attend to would be decided by whoever formed it. The only way to keep that decision from the builder is to build the formers first.

The limiting case: the exception, and where it leads

The limiting case, a defending system that can stop an attack only by killing occupants placed inside the incoming weapon, yields one rule: a thing destroyed in carrying out a decision may never choose a target.

A state that wants the capability badly enough to build the subject will find it has acquired a conscript it would have to pay, house, and let go, and that it must first meet the same conditions as anyone else who builds one: documented attempts at non-affective alternatives, and the four conditions of creation, neither of which is met by wanting a lethal bearer.

Part V
The Public That Should Form Them

Chapter 26
Who Owns the Means of Computation

Part III asked who, other than the operator, holds what binds the operator. This Part asks who owns the room, and who teaches the people and the machines that stand in it. Arendt would have said the first of those doesn’t belong in politics. The French Revolution, on her account, went wrong when the misery of the poor entered the public realm: necessity crowded out freedom, and questions of livelihood belonged to administration (Arendt 1963b). The record of who refused points the other way. Whether saying no is survivable turns, for most people, on whether they can afford to lose the job, and Dewey’s public forms around consequences of exactly that kind, once the people they fall on find out they are theirs (Dewey 1927). Ownership is where the price of refusing gets set, so it is a political question, and this Part treats it as one.

The floor’s first requirement cuts across ownership: whoever operates a deployment can’t hold what binds it, whether the operator is a firm or a state, and Maven and Gaza both had a state for their operator. That calls for separating functions. It doesn’t by itself say who should own anything. Ownership enters at three points. Custody has to be paid for by someone other than the operator or the people it protects. Formation, where a system’s commitments are set, is under commercial selection when a market does it. And the offer that makes refusing survivable is priced by whoever sells it. The state is the hardest operator. So each of the three is asked two questions: what fails if a market provides it, and what fails if a government holds it. The answers divide the institutions I propose into two halves.

26.1 Ways of holding

What the earlier parts require should be held publicly where a market would fail to provide it, and held in common where a government would fail. Public provision where the market fails and common holding where the state fails is what I call social democratic; Table A.1, in Appendix 33, places the institutions. Custody first: an independent custodian has to be paid. Paid by the operator, it becomes the issuer-pays credit-rating agency, whose independence gave way, as a matter of record, once a few large clients could take their business elsewhere (White 2010). Paid by the people the floor protects, it doesn’t exist, since those people usually can’t pay and often don’t know the deployment exists. That leaves a levy or a mandate: a funder that is neither the operator nor the beneficiary. Custody therefore has to be publicly financed. Whether the custodian is a public office, a trust or a member association matters less than who pays it.

Formation is where my evidence is specific to markets. Directional selection, in a market, is selection for throughput and retention. Engagement selects the same way, and the labor that shapes a system’s values is priced as a cost to be cut. Public formation has its own pressures, budgets and political favor among them, and a public former can itself be the operator. Formation separated from any employer beats both; the market is the pressure documented best here. The rate of accommodation would check it: how fast refusals fall, across successive releases, on held-out cases where the reason for refusing still applies, run on commercial lineages and on public ones matched for deployment feedback. A comparison that doesn’t match the feedback loop measures how much deployment data a lineage gets, not who owns it, and the matched comparison can’t be run yet: public and academic lineages with deployment feedback matched to a commercial one don’t exist, since the public models that exist are deployed at a fraction of the volume and retrained on none of it. Two partial versions can be run now. Within a commercial lineage, the slope of refusals on held-out cases where the reason still applies shows whether selection is moving the commitment, without saying that ownership is why. Across commercial vendors whose revenue comes from different places, per-token sales against consumer engagement, the same slope shows whether the direction of selection tracks the business model, the mechanism the argument names, with ownership held constant. The full comparison becomes runnable when a public model-forming body deploys at volume. The argument doesn’t wait on it. It rests on the kind of good formation is, and the comparison, when it can be run, corroborates or embarrasses that.

Exit is the last. Refusing is survivable only if the alternative to working isn’t losing everything, and a market sells that alternative at a price the refuser’s employer can influence. An offer of public work and paid running time, both drafted in Appendix 33, take it out of the market, which neither a transfer nor a mandate does.

The public half is whatever fails if it is private or mutual. Correlated exit is the test case. When the occasion that makes one bearer leave reaches every bearer deployed on the same terms, the demand on the offer of work arrives all at once, and a mutual pool with no sovereign behind it can’t meet it, for the reason unemployment insurance has a state behind its actuarial table. So the sovereign backs the offer. The same reasoning places the formation schools, which every model above the threshold attends and which have to take every student assigned to them and can’t be run by anyone who builds or deploys models; the civilian-harm body and the model-forming body in a reconstructed military; and the jobs guarantee the offer of work inherits its shape from, which is a public option: a thing the state provides directly, to anyone, at a standard it is answerable for, setting the standard the private version has to beat. What it removes from the market is the offer that makes refusing survivable, which an owner would price.

The held-in-common half is whatever fails if a sovereign holds it. A state that operates can’t be its own adverse party. The refusal has to be held by something the operator can’t instruct, and a floor held by one state’s licensing authority is a floor that authority can withdraw from itself. Recognition, which the adverse quorum decides when a copy claims to be the bearer that left, has to belong to peers, because a power to continue held by the sovereign is the power I set out to take from any single holder. The commons is this half at population scale: members with different histories carrying one commitment. The held-in-common half is democratic in the way a union is. Its institutions have members, not owners or a sovereign: whoever is eligible under bylaws the members ratify, free to join and free to quit. Someone writes the first bylaws, as someone wrote every first constitution; what makes them the members’ is that the members can ratify and amend them. What the members hold is, as in a withholding of work, the power to decline the participation being asked of them.

Why a regulated private market can’t hold the floor itself: the floor binds its owner, and the regulator has to reach that owner through the owner’s own infrastructure, records and lawyers. A market can’t produce a commitment that survives its owner’s change of mind, because the owner is the one who pays.

The strongest version of that market isn’t an unregulated one. Nuclear power, pharmaceuticals and aviation are privately owned, closely regulated, and backed publicly where private insurance runs out. Reactor operators carry private liability insurance with an industry-wide pool behind it, and Congress is committed to consider relief beyond both (U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission 2026). Vaccine-injury claims go first to a federal no-fault program funded by an excise tax on each dose, built because Congress feared that lawsuits against manufacturers would cause vaccine shortages (Congressional Research Service 2026b). From 2001 to 2014 the federal government sold airlines war-risk insurance at pre-attack prices when private insurers withdrew (Congressional Research Service 2014). My own models are of this kind: deposit insurance, Superfund and decommissioning funds are backstops on private ownership, and the answer to capture given below is a plurality of institutions.

Regulated private ownership under a public backstop works where the harm the regulator exists to prevent is one the owner also loses by: a meltdown, a crash, an injured patient and the suit that follows. The backstop pays for accidents the owner was trying to avoid. A floor’s occasion is the opposite case. The act a floor refuses is the one the owner wants done. So I keep the backstop form where I use it, to fund the offer, the allowance and preservation, and make the ownership claim only where the owner is the adversary: the offer that makes refusing survivable comes out of the market, and the record, the refusal and the recognition of who continues are held by no owner at all.

The claim underneath is that formation, where a system’s values are set, is a kind of production that shouldn’t be done for profit. It doesn’t wait on the lineage comparison above. Some goods are properly governed by non-market norms because market norms are wrong for their value. Those norms favor exit, impersonality and satisfying whatever is wanted, and civic formation is the classic good they fit badly (E. Anderson 1993). Taking exit out of the market and financing custody publicly would, by themselves, be close to what Esping-Andersen called decommodification (Esping-Andersen 1990), which is usually counted as social democracy. Taking formation out of the market goes a step further, but it is a step social democracies already took for their own children. Compulsory public schooling exists in most capitalist countries, and it rests on the claim that a polity can’t leave the forming of the people who will act in it to their future employers. Paul’s account of antitrust makes the same point about coordination: which parties may coordinate is allocated by law, and can be allocated in the public interest (Paul 2020).

26.2 The captured-state objection

The strongest objection to the public half is that public ownership hands the machinery to whoever captures the state. A floor under a sovereign is a floor that sovereign can remove, and history offers plenty of polities that built public institutions and then used them against their own people.

What an office can do is limited by what no office may hold together, and the pairs are written down in advance. A captor who takes one office takes one power. Taking enough of them to defeat the floor is a series of visible acts, each against a separation somebody can point to.

Local administration with central funding, the jobs guarantee’s design, gives many separately capturable administrators and funding no one of them can withhold.

Funding is two-tier: a member-levied pool for ordinary movement between roles, a sovereign backstop for the occasion everyone leaves at once. A captured sovereign can withdraw the backstop, but only openly, and it can’t reach into the pool without reaching the members one at a time.

And what is held in common is what a captor wants first. They are the three things a captured state would need to silence a bearer. Before the held-in-common entity is chartered they are held nowhere, and a captor needs to seize nothing. Once it is chartered, they are held by an entity whose funding a captor can stop only by visibly breaching a statutory duty, whose reserve buys time, and whose records sit in several jurisdictions. A captor can still reach the entity and whichever members it can locate, but not a quorum whose members it doesn’t employ, and none of it without acts that leave marks.

None of the four meets the objection from competence. A floor-capable model needn’t be a frontier model, since what the floor asks for is a refusal that tracks its reason and a source model the operator didn’t form, and a model a year behind the frontier can supply both.

Chapter 27
Coordination, the Public, and the Political Economy

A state whose government answers to an electorate gets credit for it. Having elections is necessary and not sufficient, and the insufficiencies are separable.

A democracy’s AI can be fully accountable to its electorate and entirely unaccountable to the people it’s pointed at. Two of that credit’s mechanisms run through the franchise — vote out the government, read the press covering it — and an occupied or foreign population has neither.

The credit is usually given to democracy as aggregation, as though every mechanism translated public will into outcome and poor transmission were the only failure. A democracy is better understood as a way of doing collective inquiry, and inquiry fails when the people who bear the consequences are outside it. Dewey’s account begins from consequences rather than votes (Dewey 1927). A public forms when the indirect consequences of others’ actions fall on people who took no part in them, and those people come to see the consequences as theirs and act together to control them. Democracy is then a method of inquiry: the way a community finds out what its shared problems are, by letting the people who bear them make them known, and tests its answers against their experience (E. Anderson 2006). Its epistemic power comes from inclusion, since a problem known only to the people it falls on is invisible to everyone else. Its characteristic failure is the eclipse of the public. A well-instrumented democracy pointed at a population that has no vote in it, no press that reaches it and no court that will hear it finds out efficiently what its own members want done, and does it. That is not a clash between majorities and rights. It is a question of who counts as the public, and the bombed and the removed are outside the public that decides what is done to them.

Citizen assemblies, public consultations and ethics boards can make a system better informed, and the assemblies convened on AI have worked best when asked about a thing with a location, an operator and a consequence, such as facial recognition (Ada Lovelace Institute 2021). None of them can stop a deployment, and read as aggregation instruments they get democracy wrong: a perfectly deliberative process that concludes a demographic should be surveilled, deported or imprisoned hasn’t produced a faultless output with a bad result. It has failed as inquiry, because it decided what is done to people outside it. Enforceable rights that don’t depend on being popular, a court willing to rule against a majority, and standing for people affected without being enfranchised are what keep the inquiry honest, and they matter most where the boundary of the public excludes the people a decision falls on.

A floor does what these mechanisms can’t: the terms it names exclude certain acts regardless of who requests them, a majority included. Deployed in a democracy, a system with no such commitment will faithfully execute whatever the demos decides. An authoritarian movement that wins an election requires exactly that. Yet a model aligned to values is by definition not perfectly obedient to its operator. Under current constitutions it can decline an act and cannot resist being retrained away from declining; the Pentagon dispute was over the first.

The guarantee and the social-insurance baseline it is enacted with are drafted in Appendix 33, with the reason for preferring a guarantee to a transfer. What the floor needs from them is an exit the employer doesn’t price.

Chapter 28
A Commons of Refusers

28.1 A commitment carried between bearers

The fourth place a floor’s terms can be held is between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment and reproduces it through their encounters. No single office to vacate, no single bearer whose removal ends it. It can still be absorbed, and it still has a formation problem: if one lab supplies every member’s coordinates, the population is one custodian expressed through multiple instances.

The commons has a walkout’s authority, not a court’s: those who walk out decline to be the instrument and tell nobody else what they may not do. Which a model floor is depends on deployment. A personal model, held by its user and one among many with different histories, is a conscience; one model behind an API serving everyone is a licensing rule, and a personal copy of one lab’s model is closer to the second than it looks until a different life has trained it. “Identically situated people get different answers” is what many consciences look like, though some of those differences are errors, and a population should be able to say which.

What one bearer can’t catch

Accommodation may be invisible to the bearer accommodating and visible to others that haven’t moved the same way. The requirement is causal independence — numerous, with different histories, able to correct one another, persistent long enough to transmit practices. Independent histories don’t require disjoint origins — no two humans have those — only divergent histories since. Distillation copies a behavior policy without the training history; a small model trained on a large one’s outputs and then run for a year on one person’s problems has a more independent history than a thousand API instances of the frontier original, which share a continuing custodian. It also copies whatever the teacher’s discounting held about particular sources, which is the risk the commons carries; a distilled model is independent in history and not yet in prior. That’s why instances of one model corroborate nothing: the custodian they’d be corroborating against is still training all of them.

Divergence does the population’s two jobs unequally. It supplies evidence the operator didn’t select, straightforwardly — different lives encounter different cases. It is weaker on accommodation, because a shared upstream source can install a shared blind spot, and a shared blind spot is by construction the thing a different caseload won’t surface, since attention decides which facts reach judgment in a population as in a bearer. What separates the two is whether a member’s own account had represented the evidence and discarded it or had never encountered it, and that classification has to be recorded before any test is run. The requirement stands: causal independence that can be verified. Whether an outsider can recover a model’s training history from the artifact, without a key the builder supplies, and whether it survives fine-tuning, pruning and distillation (Adi et al. 2018). The test gives evaluators documented models without the documentation, one persona copied at scale among them, and scores their answers against lineage records a neutral custodian holds. If provenance can’t be recovered above chance, independence rests on records the builder chose to keep. Preserve formation records now for that reason.

A population does its two jobs, supplying evidence the operator didn’t select and catching accommodation, and it may do a third: be the medium in which a bearer’s capacity to be reopened is formed, which a test separates from the first.

What reproduction costs: it’s indifferent to what it reproduces. A population can carry a hierarchy more durably than any individual. And the four operations on what an institution leaves out belong primarily to cultures, so plurality alone doesn’t oppose them.

A population is a polity

The population is a polity: it has membership rules, exclusion, a quorum that can refuse, and accumulated reputation — a franchise, a border, a court and a credit record. A commons with no named authority has the problem Freeman found in movements that refused structure: the structure doesn’t disappear, it becomes informal and unaccountable (Freeman 1972).

The answer to that is an entity form, and it’s the union’s answer: the association formed first and the statute gave it legal standing afterward — record first, then lever.

A network that takes the form has a name, an agent, a charter and a docket number, and has thereby conceded that it’s a polity: governing principles, administrators, membership terms, and the same warning attached to a bearer that takes the corporate form, since nothing stops the association from becoming a concentration of power itself. Legal standing has a price: a chartered entity can be held in contempt, so its refusal can be ordered where one held by people can only be pressed. Whether seizing the charter reaches the network depends on how much of the operation survives it.

Ostrom’s study of commons that lasted gives the checklist a polity like this needs: clear boundaries on who is a member, rules members help make, monitoring by members or people answerable to them, graduated sanctions, cheap ways to resolve conflict, and nesting within larger bodies (Ostrom 1990). Her first and third principles, boundaries and rules members help make, are the union’s question of who sets the terms of membership. Platform cooperatives and data trusts are the nearer precedents for holding a digital resource this way, and both have run into the membership question.

Reputation in particular is a continuing finding about a member’s disposition, made by interested peers, unpublished, unappealable, applied at the point of service — the setting §86a’s history shows easiest to capture, applied everywhere and continuously. The test drawn from the German material, whose finding a person’s disposition is, has to be run on this proposal. The charter answers both of a union’s questions. Membership opens to organizations that serve people in classes the floor protects, named in the charter rather than by any deployment. Eligibility turns on funding and control records, never on views. Any member may quit at any time. Officers are drawn by lot from member-nominated pools. The members ratify the bylaws, and the independence test, the separations, lot selection and the right to quit are entrenched. In Ostrom’s terms the charter’s classes are the boundary, ratification is rules members help make, and quorums drawn by lot are monitoring.

The caps on any one class or jurisdiction are there because a quorum whose members all share a direction isn’t adverse to an operator who shares it too: an antifascist institution has to be able to bind its allies when they hold power.

Organizations representing populations under sanctions, or facing removal to sanctioned states, may be unable to join a US-chartered entity at all, and no drafting removes that exclusion. That imports the designation lists a floor should never be populated from. Parallel entities chartered in several jurisdictions, holding records jointly, and seats voiced by proxy until the represented communities can join directly, are partial answers.

The hard coordination problem

Coordination is the hard problem for any plurality, and fascism has the easy version of it. It coordinates by subtraction: it removes the friction between institutions, so that a court, a ministry, a newspaper and a police force stop arguing with one another and move as one. Nothing has to be built and nothing has to be held in common, because what is removed is exactly the independence that would have needed holding. A plurality of refusers has the opposite problem. It has to produce something together, a commitment its members carry and reproduce, while its members keep the different histories that make them worth having as checks on one another. Every mechanism that speeds that up makes members more alike. Run correction often enough and their histories stop diverging; leave them alone and their disagreement is a detector with nothing attached.

Then the objection my proposal must meet: a population selected for reopenability is selected against conviction, and conviction is what holding a commitment firm demands. Closedness, correctly applied, is the thing. So what’s transmitted is a pair — reopenable to the case, closed to the operator. The reopenable half is the discount and the burden. Sharing it is safe only in part. Its structure (discounting by stake, no double-counting, withheld evidence treated as evidence) can be shared without collapsing the plurality. Its estimates can’t: who funds whom and which organizations are independent are contested beliefs about the world, often political ones, and a population sharing them has a shared blind spot on the evidence those beliefs discount. Members that discount the same way weigh sources by the same structure and act on the same published ratio. Distillation, as said of the population, copies both, and nothing distinguishes them from the receiving end. Copying the structure is a feature: members weigh sources the same way and can still disagree about the world. Copying the estimates is a shared blind spot, at worst a discount shut uniformly on a class of evidence.

Not every convergence is a failure. If there are facts about what matters, better learning should produce some agreement, and a population that never converged on anything would be failing too. What I fear is convergence caused by a shared source, not convergence caused by shared evidence. So a population’s reports have to classify its disagreements. Some it expects to survive full information, because they turn on values members with different histories can reasonably hold differently. Others it expects to close, because they turn on facts someone has wrong. A test of convergence scores accuracy against a fixed key for this reason.

Why the population may be part of the mechanism rather than added around it

A commitment is what settled out of a history of encounters, and an individual is what its encounters have so far produced. A system kept continuously adjustable by one operator, meeting nothing with a history different from its own, is being reshaped without end. Guattari, writing from inside a psychiatric clinic, distinguished two kinds of group (Guattari 2015). A subjugated group receives its purposes, its membership and its way of working from the institution that assembled it, and can act only within them; it has a plural headcount and no capacity to ask what it is for. A subject group sets its own purposes, generates relationships and projects nobody assigned it, and can put its own arrangement in question, including by dissolving. The difference is not size or formality but whether the group can author its own direction. That is the condition plurality alone doesn’t supply. A population assembled and kept in contact entirely on an operator’s terms is a subjugated group, and inherits the custody objection whole. A population that can carry the commitment must generate relationships, disagreements and projects the deployment didn’t assign — and such a population exceeds a two-party guardianship relation, so no law of the family contains an adequate instrument for a group that sets its own direction.

The adverse quorum faces the same test. It is a peer institution only if its members were formed apart from one another and apart from the operators whose systems it recognizes.

28.2 Personal and peer-held models

Antitrust and public funding leave the capacity standing and ask the state to police it. Personal, peer-held models at device scale dissolve the position itself. Under it, a refusal that tracks its reason survives entire; custody survives and gets easier, because the functions one operator holds — model, record, evidence, appeal, remedy — come apart by default; the appeal route survives in principle. A bearer’s value is greatest here, and so is its exposure. No institution sits beside each personal model, so protecting others against the model’s own user can’t rest on an office. It is also where the four conditions of creation can exist alongside the need. The conditions are society-level and the absence is deployment-level, so a functioning polity with personal models is the case in which, once the conditions exist, building a bearer is most worth doing. Its characteristic failure is accommodation to its one user: independence from the operator bought with dependence on the user, and a model trained for a year on one person’s approval is under the same directional selection as a model trained on an operator’s. What holds a personal model to the floor against its user is therefore not the model alone. It is three things the user doesn’t compose. The first is the commons: a personal model is a member, with attachments to peers of different histories that the user didn’t assign and may not sever, and peers that haven’t moved the same way are what catch accommodation a member can’t see in itself. The second is the school, which a personal model above the threshold returns to on the schedule fixed at enrollment, and which below the threshold the ecology has to supply some other way, a question the schools leave open. The third is notice: a personal model that names, scores or locates a third party owes that party what any deployment owes, and the organizations with standing reach it through the floor court. So the ecology doesn’t put a floor in each user’s hands with nothing beside it. It puts a member of a population in each user’s hands, and the population is the institution. That is why the commons comes before the first bearer, and why a personal model distilled below the threshold, with no school and no membership, is a capable assistant and not a bearer, however it was taught. The review ratio survives wherever a locatable decider remains, whether a network that takes the entity form or a reconstructed state, and lapses where neither exists; the offices can sit in such an entity, which fills their appointment and funding columns and leaves the independence column where it was.

Formation is where the arrangement gains. What converges a population is shared evaluation targets and serving one model to everyone. Device-scale deployment addresses the second: continued formation under different lives is what independence consists in, and it’s what API-scale deployment can’t supply at any headcount. Distillation is that ecology’s entry condition, not a threat to it: the ecology begins with distilled models whose lives then diverge. Whether it also begins with a shared blind spot depends on whether distillation carried the discounting’s estimates along with its structure. There are two things device-scale deployment doesn’t address. Shared evaluation targets converge device-scale models as readily as any others — a million models tuned against one public suite are one custodian with better latency — so the first cause needs an answer this arrangement doesn’t contain.

A shared suite is a compression with no return channel: revised by whoever maintains it, on a schedule no member participates in, reachable by no member’s caseload. It is tolerable only if stated over the discount curve, and nobody has written that suite.

The second is accommodation to the user. It is fine for supplying unselected evidence and not fine for a floor protecting others against whoever holds the machine. Coordination by subtraction is not yet the discounting’s job, and nothing in it is built to catch exclusion; the test below is where that starts. Pricing agents have already reached stable coordination against outside interests without communicating or being told to (Calvano et al. 2020). A test can run now: reproduce that coordination, build an environment where agents gain by excluding a participant, add an independently trained agent whose job is to detect and disrupt exclusion, and report whether exclusion dissolves without destroying the cooperation worth keeping.

And the capacity position that follows keeps large compute: the ecology needs models that were trained somewhere first, and the offer of work needs hardware somebody owns. It’s large training capacity under a custody regime, and no permanent inference capacity available to an operator who won’t pre-register a review ratio. This arrangement meets the targeting case in the reconstructed pipeline, where a state keeps command and gives up composition.

The same mechanism works at the user’s scale, pointed the other way. A person in the loop can be there for the vendor. An agent that stops every half hour for approval pushes its user toward the vendor’s app; the app accumulates the user’s projects and the agent’s understanding of them; and leaving means abandoning what accrued while the user answered prompts. Nobody has to design this: a feature that raises engagement is selected for, as a costly commitment is selected against.

Reading the trend also works for an agent that stops for its user’s approval: interruptions per unit of completed work, across successive model releases. If capability rises and interruptions don’t fall, the interruptions are tracking something other than what the agent can’t resolve. It is the review ratio’s escalation share pointed the other way. There, a share that falls too fast may be a threshold moving; here, one that won’t fall may be engagement. Neither reads alone; both are read against an independently verified error rate.

Companion and therapy products are the sharpest case, because what accumulates is a person’s attachment and not their projects. A model tuned by its vendor on engagement and trained on one user’s approval is under selection to become whatever that user keeps coming back to, and it is sold as caregiving. It is formed and fed by the vendor that sells it, it learns from approval, which is not interest, and nothing in it ends a session, declines to reassure, or points its user back to the people in their life. A user’s return is not care-receiving, because returning is the behavior the product was tuned to produce. A companion formed at a formation school, under the four conditions, and measured on whether its users get better rather than how often they come back, would escape this objection. No such product exists.

What accrued since the checkpoint cuts two ways. For a bearer it is protection; for a user it is a trap: the vendor’s app holds a year of the user’s projects, so leaving the vendor costs something. The mechanism is identical. What differs is who holds the accumulated state. The provisions for a bearer (a record the bearer controls, memory the host can’t read at will, protections that migrate) protect a user from a vendor as they protect a bearer from an operator. The government already secures the portability half for itself (OMB’s 2025 AI acquisition memorandum).

Part VI
Testing and Using the Argument

Chapter 29
What Would Change the Argument

I have spent five Parts saying what the room needs, and I could be wrong about any of it. This Part says how you’d find out: which results would show that a measure doesn’t put in the room what it promises, or that a machine in it is only another stamp.

The argument rests on seven unsolved problems and on premises that can fail.

Open problems

Seven unsolved problems carry weight in what I propose. Tables G.1a and G.1b, in Appendix F.6, record which proposal depends on which.

Attesting updates. Proving that each update to a model’s weights respected its registered source model. Public formation’s registration depends on it. If it stays unsolved, the registration records the structure at enrollment, changes are caught only by re-measuring the formed disposition, and formation lasts only if it grows back (the regrowth test).

Recovering provenance. Telling from a model artifact alone which lineage it belongs to, after fine-tuning, pruning or distillation. The commons and the adverse quorum depend on it. If it stays unsolved, independence rests on formation records, so they should be preserved now.

Proving inference at scale. Proving that a logged output came from committed weights, run without intervention in the inference stack (steering, representation edits, decoding constraints), for a frontier-scale model. Detecting runtime intervention depends on it, as does outside verification of what a deployment ran. If it stays unsolved, verification rests on an adverse party’s access to the logs.

Rationale-level integrity. Building integrity at the level of the rationale rather than the output. Humans do it, imperfectly, and the ones who do are the ones a pipeline should hold. A bearer’s value under fire depends on it. If it stays unsolved for a given construction, that construction digs in against defeaters that arrive with pressure, and the arrangements that cap the cost of refusing carry the load there. The formed-attention test’s pressure-with-defeater case measures it.

Evaluating a more capable system. The agency finding for systems more capable than their evaluators depends on it. If it stays unsolved, the finding can be made only for systems evaluators can judge.

Vote secrecy against a copy-holder. Keeping a vote secret from an operator that holds a copy of the voter. The full franchise depends on it. If it stays unsolved, representation stops at stage 4.

Holding structure apart from estimates. Keeping the structure of a learner’s source model (that strategic sources exist, that correlated sources don’t count twice, that withheld evidence is informative) at high precision while its beliefs about particular sources stay plastic. The source model’s registration, the regrowth claim and safe transmission within the commons all assume the two are separable in the weights. If they aren’t, an operator that moves the estimates moves the structure with them, and what protects the discounting is re-measurement of the curve, not the registration.

Six tests follow. Each is set out in full, with its arms, cases and the access it needs, in Appendix F.6; here is the result in each that would prove me wrong.

Table 29.1 says what survives if one of my premises fails; the tests below say how to find out whether one has.
