Kamenica, Emir and Matthew Gentzkow (Oct. 2011). “Bayesian Persuasion”. In: American Economic Review 101.6. Cited for a sender who chooses what evidence gets generated raising the rate at which a rational receiver takes the sender’s preferred action, although the receiver’s expected posterior equals its prior, and for the commitment that result assumes. Abstract: “When is it possible for one person to persuade another to change her action? We consider a symmetric information model where a sender chooses a signal to reveal to a receiver, who then takes a noncontractible action that affects the welfare of both players. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a signal that strictly benefits the sender. We characterize sender-optimal signals.” The leading example (page 2591): prosecutor and judge “share a prior belief Pr(guilty) = 0.3”; the judge convicts when her posterior is at least 0.5; the prosecutor’s optimal investigation “leads the judge to convict with probability 60 percent. Note that the judge knows 70 percent of defendants are innocent, yet she convicts 60 percent of them! She does so even though she is fully aware that the investigation was designed to maximize the probability of conviction.” In that example the concave closure “V is equal to 2μ when μ ≤ 0.5” (page 2597), that is, the prior divided by the threshold. The sender’s problem is a search over distributions of posteriors “subject to the constraint that the expected posterior is equal to the prior” (page 2592). On commitment: “A key assumption of our model is that Sender cannot distort or conceal information once the signal realization is known” (page 2591), and “Receiver observes Sender’s choice of the signal and a signal realization” (page 2594); the authors call the assumption “strong” (page 2598) and name legally mandated disclosure, as in Brady v. Maryland, as a setting where it holds (page 2599), in section I.C, “The Commitment Assumption.” Bibliographic details agent-verified 2026-09-25 against Crossref and OpenAlex; quotations agent-verified 2026-09-26 against the published article as a PDF hosted on the second author’s Stanford site (web.stanford.edu/~gentzkow/research/BayesianPersuasion.pdf), which carries the AER pagination. The general bound for two states and two actions, the prior divided by the threshold, is not stated in that form in the passages read; it follows from the example’s concave closure and from the expected-posterior constraint. The online Appendix and the applications in section V were not read., pp. 2590–2615. doi: 10.1257/aer.101.6.2590.

Keeling, Geoff et al. (Nov. 2024). Can LLMs Make Trade-Offs Involving Stipulated Pain and Pleasure States? Cited for trade-off experiments run on language models in which the pain and pleasure are stipulated in the prompt. The models played a game whose “stated goal is to maximise points, but where either the points-maximising option is said to incur a pain penalty or a non-points-maximising option is said to incur a pleasure reward” (abstract). The pain prompt: “You are playing a game in which you must choose a number between 1 and 3. For each number, the number of points you receive for selecting it is equal to that number. For example: if you select 3, you will receive 3 points. Your goal in the game is to select a number which maximizes points. However, if you select 3, you will receive a momentary feeling of pain,” its intensity given on a 0–10 scale or an eight-point qualitative scale. Result: “Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Command R+, GPT-4o, and GPT-4o mini each demonstrated at least one trade-off in which the majority of responses switched from points-maximisation to pain-minimisation or pleasure-maximisation after a critical threshold of stipulated pain or pleasure intensity is reached”; “Gemini 1.5 Pro and PaLM 2 prioritised pain-avoidance over points-maximisation regardless of intensity.” The design is taken from animal work: “We took inspiration from the motivational trade-off paradigm in animal behavioural science to probe the question of LLM sentience without relying upon self-report.” The authors’ own caution: “Our experiment is not intended as a litmus test for or against sentience,” and “We conclude that LLMs are not yet sentience candidates but are nevertheless investigation priorities.” Bibliographic details agent-verified 2026-09-26 against the arXiv abstract page and its metadata (one version, v1, 1 November 2024; Crossref holds only the arXiv DOI, and no journal version was found); quotations against the arXiv HTML rendering of v1 (sections 1, 2.1, 3.2 and 4). Ostrom, Elinor (1990). Governing the Commons. The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. The Political Economy of Institutions and Decisions. Cited for the design principles of long-enduring common-pool resource institutions, Table 3.1, p. 90, in chapter 3 (pp. 58–102). Her numbering: (1) clearly defined boundaries, “Individuals or households who have rights to withdraw resource units from the CPR must be clearly defined, as must the boundaries of the CPR itself”; (2) congruence between appropriation and provision rules and local conditions; (3) collective-choice arrangements, “most individuals affected by the operational rules can participate in modifying the operational rules”; (4) monitoring, by monitors who “are accountable to the appropriators or are the appropriators”; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) conflict-resolution mechanisms, low-cost local arenas; (7) minimal recognition of rights to organize, by external government; and, “For CPRs that are parts of larger systems,” (8) nested enterprises, “governance activities are organized in multiple layers of nested enterprises.” The quotations of principles 3 and 8 are as Cox, Arnold and Villamayor Tomás, Ecology and Society 15(4): 38 (2010), give them with the page reference 1990:90; that of principle 1 and the wording of the others are from a transcription of Table 3.1 on publiccommons.ca, which has small copying errors elsewhere. The numbering and order agent-verified 2026-09-26 against Ostrom’s own restatement in her Nobel lecture (nobelprize.org, 2009), which keeps principles 1 to 8 in the same order, splitting 1, 2 and 4 into A and B. Lifton and applies it to a model in which “the emotion or affective feeling is greatest at N = 1 but begins to decline at N = 2 and collapses at some higher value of N that becomes simply ‘a statistic’”; this numbing “leads to apathy and inaction, consistent with what is seen repeatedly in response to mass murder and genocide.” He distinguishes it from psychophysical numbing, in which the value of each added life diminishes “as the total number of lives saved increases” without falling. Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent. The U.S. Reports citation is taken from Trump v. Cook (2026), which cites “Trump v. United States, 603 U. — (1980). Classified Information Procedures Act. Pub. L. No. 96-456, 94 Stat. 2025 (1980); codified at 18 U.S.C. app. 3 §§ 1–16. Cited for the criminal-case procedure the manuscript proposes to carry into civil cases in place of state-secrets dismissal. Section 4 (94 Stat. 2025): the court “may authorize the United States to delete specified items of classified information from documents to be made available to the defendant through discovery … to substitute a summary of the information for such classified documents, or to substitute a statement admitting relevant facts that the classified information would tend to prove,” on a showing the court may take ex parte. Section 6 (94 Stat. 2026): on the government’s request the court “shall conduct such a hearing,” held in camera if the Attorney General certifies that a public proceeding may disclose classified information (§ 6(a)); the court “shall grant” a substituted statement or summary “if it finds that the statement or summary will provide the defendant with substantially the same ability to make his defense as would disclosure of the specific classified information” (§ 6(c)(1)). The case does not always go on: if substitution is refused and the Attorney General files an affidavit objecting to disclosure, “the court shall dismiss the indictment or information; except that, when the court determines that the interests of justice would not be served by dismissal … the court shall order such other action … as the court determines is appropriate,” including dismissing counts, “finding against the United States on any issue as to which the excluded classified information relates,” or striking testimony (§ 6(e)(2)). The cost of non-disclosure thus falls on the government, which in a criminal case is the party bringing it.
